<issue identifier="MM-420">
<title>Notify 6/9: wallet Notification Service Extension — decrypt-and-render + unverified notice</title>
<description>
Phase 6 of the <issue id="b95fcd23-95fa-43f6-86a6-81defb9dda77" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311/e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-custos-apns">MM-311</issue> notification relay. Implementation details: `docs/design-plans/2026-07-17-notification-relay-implementation.md`.

## Scope

* **Xcode template:** the forked `scripts/ios/project.yml` (shared by both apps, rendered on every `cargo tauri ios init`) gains an NSE target (`{{app.name}}_NSE`, `type: app-extension`, **Swift-only** — no second Rust staticlib; decryption is CryptoKit, ~200 lines) and `keychain-access-groups` entitlements on both targets. `just ios-template-check` learns the new invariants (NSE target present, entitlements wired) so a template re-render can't silently drop them.
* **NSE behavior:** on `mutable-content: 1` delivery, load the notification private key + pinned sender set from the shared keychain group, HPKE-open (`P256_SHA256_AES_GCM_256`, `authenticatedBy:` the key named by `kid`, `info = "ezpds/notify/1"`), replace placeholder title/body with plaintext.
* **Failure path** (iOS cannot suppress an alert push): unknown `kid`, open failure, or post-reboot locked keychain → render the explicit **unverified notice** ("Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance") — never authentic-looking content — and write a diagnostic breadcrumb to a shared app-group container.
* **Diagnostics surface:** the app reads the breadcrumbs and surfaces repeated failures in Settings (key desync / misbehaving relay made visible, per the design doc).
* **Interop check:** on-device XCTest opens the `crates/crypto` golden fixtures with CryptoKit — the cross-implementation verification the fixtures were built for.

## Acceptance

* On-device demo: sealed push from a real Custos renders decrypted content; junk/replayed-junk payload renders the unverified notice; fixture cross-check passes.
* ios-pr-check lane green (template regeneration + postinit + ios-check with the new invariants).
</description>

<label>Security</label>
<label>Feature</label>
<label>Mobile: Identity Wallet</label>

<title>E2E-encrypted notification relay for self-hosted Custos (APNs)</title>
<description>
Implement the notification relay designed in [docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md](<https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/blob/main/docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md>) (design PR <pull-request id="34230e45-6259-4c9a-b58d-6b135adf84e3" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/review/design-exploration-e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-327f880332d1">malpercio-dev/ezpds#207</pull-request>, **merged** — the doc on `main` is the source of truth and incorporates the review hardening: claim-code enrollment authorization for the official relay, versioned sender keys with re-pin/revocation semantics, explicit v1 replay acceptance, unverified-notice rendering for unauthenticated payloads, per-handle APNs topics, serialized-request padding budget, and the post-reboot keychain window).

## Problem

Self-hosted Custos instances need to deliver push notifications to the official iOS apps (Obsign, admin-companion). APNs auth keys are bundle-ID-bound, so self-hosters cannot push directly — a relay is structurally required. The design makes that relay a **blind courier**: trusted for availability only.

## Architecture (see design doc for full detail)

* **Confidentiality:** payloads HPKE-sealed (RFC 9180, DHKEM-P256 + AES-GCM) to a per-device notification key; decrypted on-device by a Notification Service Extension (`mutable-content: 1`). Neither the relay nor Apple sees plaintext.
* **Integrity:** HPKE Auth mode with pinned, versioned per-instance sender keys — the relay cannot forge authenticated content (it can generate detectable junk pushes and replay; v1 accepts duplicates as benign).
* **Metadata minimization:** opaque push handles bound to the instance's iroh node id (no DIDs/handles/raw tokens at the relay), fixed-size padding budgeted against the serialized APNs request, optional content-free ping mode.
* **Transport:** Custos ↔ relay over iroh, new `ezpds/notify/0` ALPN, reusing the persisted node identity (`iroh_identity`) and `iroh_tunnel.rs` patterns; back-channel carries APNs `410 Unregistered` pruning feedback.
* **Sovereignty:** relay is an open-source workspace crate (`crates/notify-relay/`); any instance points at any relay via `[notifications] relay = "<node id>"`. Official relay requires a claim-code enrollment grant; open enrollment is a config option for self-run relays. Caveat: official bundle IDs require the official relay's APNs key.

## Suggested phasing

1. **Relay crate + Custos sender** — `crates/notify-relay/` (claim-code enrollment grants, handle store with per-handle APNs topic, APNs HTTP/2 client, per-node rate limits, serialized-request size validation with 4 KB boundary test) + `[notifications]` config, device notification-key registration route, versioned sender-key set, sealed-send on first trigger (agent claim pending). Loopback iroh e2e tests with mock APNs.
2. **Wallet NSE** — per-device keypair + shared keychain access group, registration in onboarding, decrypt-and-render extension, unverified-notice fallback + in-app diagnostics.
3. **Admin-companion adoption + operator docs** — ops alert triggers, self-relay runbook, metadata-minimizing ping mode.

## Open questions (from the design doc)

* Enrollment grant distribution for the official relay (ceremony mirrors admin-device pairing)
* Replay hardening beyond v1's accept-duplicates posture (per-device counter + durable replay window)
* Delivery receipts over the iroh back-channel (out of scope v1)
* Android/FCM later (envelope is provider-agnostic)

Not yet scheduled into a wave; split into per-phase issues when picked up.
</description>
</parent-issue>

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/linear-workflow

# Linear Development Workflow

This skill manages the full lifecycle of working on a Linear issue: from picking it up through opening a PR.

## Starting Work on an Issue

When the user indicates they want to work on a Linear issue (e.g., "Let's work on MM-42"):

1. **Parse the issue identifier** from the user's message. The pattern is `MM-` followed by a number.

2. **Fetch the issue details** from Linear using the `get_issue` tool with the parsed identifier. Display a brief summary to the user: title, description (truncated if long), priority, and any existing labels.

3. **Update the issue in Linear:**
   - Set the status to **"In Progress"**
   - Assign it to **"me"** (the authenticated user)

   Use the `save_issue` tool with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Progress"`, and `assignee: "me"`.

4. **Create a git branch from a fresh base** using the issue's suggested branch name:
   - The `get_issue` response includes a `branchName` field — use that as the branch name.
   - **Fetch first, then branch from the remote tip — never from a possibly-stale local HEAD:**
     `git fetch origin main && git checkout -b <branchName> origin/main`
     A stale base silently duplicates work that already merged (hours lost rebuilding an already-shipped backend is the known failure mode).
   - If the branch already exists locally, check it out, then run `git log --oneline <branchName>..origin/main` and surface to the user how far behind the base is.

5. **Verify sibling work is in the base.** If the issue depends on or overlaps sibling issues already marked Done in Linear, confirm their PRs are actually present in the branch base (e.g. `git log --oneline origin/main | grep -i mm-nnn`, or check for the files/routes they added) before concluding any related feature is "missing". **"Linear says Done but the code isn't here" is a hard stop-and-verify signal — it almost always means your base is stale, not that the feature needs building.**

6. **Confirm to the user** what happened: issue assigned, status updated, branch created/checked out (and from which base commit). Then ask what they'd like to tackle first, or summarize the issue so they can dive in.

## Opening a PR (Auto-transition to "In Review")

When the user asks to open a PR, create a pull request, or you detect that a PR is being created for a branch associated with a Linear issue:

1. **Identify the Linear issue** from the current branch name. Linear branch names typically contain the issue identifier (e.g., `malpercio/mm-42-fix-the-thing`). Extract the `MM-XXX` portion.

2. **Create the PR** as the user requests (follow normal PR creation workflow).

3. **After the PR is successfully created**, update the Linear issue:
   - Set the status to **"In Review"**
   - Attach the PR URL as a link on the issue using the `links` field in `save_issue`

   Use `save_issue` with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Review"`, and `links: [{"url": "<pr-url>", "title": "Pull Request"}]`.

4. **Confirm** to the user that the issue has been moved to "In Review" and the PR link has been attached.

## Important Notes

- Always fetch the issue first to confirm it exists and get the full `id` (UUID) needed for updates.
- If the issue is already "In Progress" and assigned, skip those updates and just create the branch.
- If branch creation fails (e.g., uncommitted changes), inform the user and suggest next steps rather than silently failing.
- The PR-to-"In Review" transition should happen automatically whenever a PR is opened during a session where the user started work on a Linear issue. Track the active issue identifier throughout the session.

## Scope

* **Xcode template:** the forked `scripts/ios/project.yml` (shared by both apps, rendered on every `cargo tauri ios init`) gains an NSE target (`{{app.name}}_NSE`, `type: app-extension`, **Swift-only** — no second Rust staticlib; decryption is CryptoKit, ~200 lines) and `keychain-access-groups` entitlements on both targets. `just ios-template-check` learns the new invariants (NSE target present, entitlements wired) so a template re-render can't silently drop them.

* **Diagnostics surface:** the app reads the breadcrumbs and surfaces repeated failures in Settings (key desync / misbehaving relay made visible, per the design doc).
* **Interop check:** on-device XCTest opens the `crates/crypto` golden fixtures with CryptoKit — the cross-implementation verification the fixtures were built for.

* On-device demo: sealed push from a real Custos renders decrypted content; junk/replayed-junk payload renders the unverified notice; fixture cross-check passes.

2	
3	[MM-311](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311) · implementation leg of
4	[docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md](2026-07-10-notification-relay.md)
5	(design PR #207, merged — that doc remains the architecture source of truth; this doc pins
6	the implementation details against the codebase and decomposes the work into issues).
7	
8	**Codebase verified: 2026-07-17** (migrations at V051, bruno seq at 123, iroh 1.0.0,
9	workspace 0.5.2).
10	
11	## Refinements to the design doc
12	
13	Three details discovered during codebase verification refine (not reverse) the design:
14	
15	1. **Registrations key on the account DID, not `devices.id`.** The design says the
16	   registration lands in "new columns/table beside `devices`" — but `devices` is a
17	   *transient pre-DID artifact*: rows are deleted inside the DID-promotion transaction
18	   (`routes/create_did.rs`) and the table FKs to `pending_accounts`. A registration FK'd
19	   there would die exactly when the account starts mattering. Wallet notification
20	   registrations therefore key on `(did, device_uuid)` where `device_uuid` is an
21	   app-generated stable identifier, are created **post-promotion** over the OAuth/DPoP
22	   channel (through the `authenticate_access` seam — the auth-seam-check applies), and are
23	   purged in `account_delete::purge_account`'s explicit FK-ordered delete list.
24	   Admin-companion registrations are a separate table keyed by `admin_devices.id`,
25	   cleaned up alongside the revoke tombstone. Pending (pre-DID) accounts get no pushes —
26	   onboarding completes with promotion, and registration is one of the first
27	   post-promotion calls.
28	2. **The ciphersuite is forced to AES-256-GCM.** CryptoKit ships exactly one P-256 HPKE
29	   suite: `HPKE.Ciphersuite.P256_SHA256_AES_GCM_256`. So the wire suite is pinned to
30	   **DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM, mode_auth** — no
31	   negotiation, ever; `v` in the envelope names the whole suite. RFC 9180's appendix has
32	   no test vector for this exact combo (A.3 is AES-128), so golden fixtures are generated
33	   from the Rust implementation, pinned in `crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/`, and
34	   cross-verified against CryptoKit by an on-device XCTest in the wallet phase.
35	3. **The v1 back-channel is the RPC response, not a server-initiated stream.** The relay
36	   calls APNs synchronously inside the push RPC, so `410 Unregistered` (and throttle/size
37	   outcomes) return in the same request/response exchange over the already-open bidi
38	   stream. No relay-initiated streams in v1 — that machinery (delivery receipts) stays
39	   out of scope, as the design already decided.
40	
41	CryptoKit's HPKE API requires **iOS 17**; the apps' deployment target currently rides
42	tauri-cli's default (13.0, nothing overridden in either `tauri.conf.json`). Decision:
43	raise `bundle > iOS > minimumSystemVersion` to `17.0` for both apps in the wallet phase.
44	Both apps are new (no installed base below 17), and a per-target split (NSE at 17, app
45	lower, runtime-gated registration) buys nothing but complexity.
46	
47	## Wire formats
48	
49	### Sealed payload (Custos → device, opaque to relay/Apple)
50	
51	Plaintext (serde_json, camelCase):
52	
53	```json
54	{ "type": "agent_claim_pending", "title": "…", "body": "…", "data": { … }, "pad": "…" }
55	```
56	
57	`pad` is a string of `0x20` bytes sized so the **serialized APNs request** lands exactly
58	on a padding bucket (below). Sealed with HPKE mode_auth:
59	
60	- suite: DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM
61	- `info = b"ezpds/notify/1"`, `aad = b""` (version binding lives in `info` + envelope `v`)
62	- sender key: the instance's static notification sender keypair named by `kid`
63	- recipient key: the device's notification public key
64	
65	### APNs payload (relay → Apple → device)
66	
67	```json
68	{
69	  "aps": { "alert": { "title": "Custos", "body": "Encrypted notification" },
70	           "mutable-content": 1 },
71	  "ezpds": { "v": 1, "kid": 3, "enc": "<b64url encapsulated key>", "ct": "<b64url ciphertext>" }
72	}
73	```
74	
75	Ping mode (later phase) replaces `aps` with `{ "content-available": 1 }` and omits
76	`ezpds` entirely.
77	
78	### Padding buckets
79	
80	Buckets are defined on the **serialized APNs JSON body**: `{1024, 2048, 3584}` bytes
81	(3584 keeps headroom under APNs' 4096 cap). Base64url expansion is deterministic
82	(`enc` = 65-byte uncompressed P-256 point → 87 chars; `ct` = plaintext + 16-byte tag),
83	so Custos computes the exact `pad` length that makes the final body hit the smallest
84	bucket ≥ the unpadded size, and refuses payloads that exceed the largest bucket. A
85	relay-side check enforces the same cap defensively, with a boundary test at exactly
86	4096 bytes.
87	
88	### Custos ↔ relay RPC (`ezpds/notify/0`)
89	
90	New ALPN beside `ezpds/iroh/0`. One JSON request per bidi stream, response JSON, stream
91	FIN delimits (the `iroh_tunnel.rs` pattern: `read_to_end` with a 64 KiB cap, 30 s
92	per-stream timeout). The dialing node's identity is `connection.remote_id()` — no
93	credential in the messages. Requests are a tagged enum:
94	
95	| request | response | notes |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| `enroll { claimCode? }` | `ok` / `denied` | idempotent; `claimCode` required unless the relay runs open enrollment |
98	| `registerHandle { apnsToken, apnsTopic }` | `{ handle }` | topic must be in the relay's served-topic set; re-registering the same token rotates the handle |
99	| `dropHandle { handle }` | `ok` | idempotent |
100	| `push { handle, kid, enc, ct, priority, ttlSecs, ping }` | `{ outcome }` | outcome ∈ `delivered · unregistered · throttled · tooLarge · notEnrolled · unknownHandle · apnsError` |

## Refinements to the design doc

1. **Registrations key on the account DID, not `devices.id`.** The design says the

lower, runtime-gated registration) buys nothing but complexity.

### Custos ↔ relay RPC (`ezpds/notify/0`)

New ALPN beside `ezpds/iroh/0`. One JSON request per bidi stream, response JSON, stream
FIN delimits (the `iroh_tunnel.rs` pattern: `read_to_end` with a 64 KiB cap, 30 s
per-stream timeout). The dialing node's identity is `connection.remote_id()` — no
credential in the messages. Requests are a tagged enum:

| request | response | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `enroll { claimCode? }` | `ok` / `denied` | idempotent; `claimCode` required unless the relay runs open enrollment |
| `registerHandle { apnsToken, apnsTopic }` | `{ handle }` | topic must be in the relay's served-topic set; re-registering the same token rotates the handle |
| `dropHandle { handle }` | `ok` | idempotent |
| `push { handle, kid, enc, ct, priority, ttlSecs, ping }` | `{ outcome }` | outcome ∈ `delivered · unregistered · throttled · tooLarge · notEnrolled · unknownHandle · apnsError` |

commit 2fe1d2c4679509129453bdb60454c313cce0211f
Author: Malpercio <107359887+malpercio-dev@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Mon Jul 27 22:01:02 2026 -0400

    Wallet: notification keys, registration and sender-key re-pinning (MM-419) (#472)
    
    * Wallet: notification keys, registration and sender-key re-pinning (MM-419)
    
    The device half of the encrypted notification relay MM-418 landed the server
    side of. Obsign generates a per-device P-256 notification key, registers it with
    each identity's Custos, and re-pins the sender keys that instance publishes.
    
    Three things are worth reviewing carefully.
    
    **The keychain surface is an accessibility class, not a new store.** The shared
    access group already exists — `org.obsign.shared` is first in the entitlement
    array, so every item already lands somewhere a Notification Service Extension
    can reach. What the extension additionally needs is
    `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, because a push arrives on a locked screen.
    `store_item_after_first_unlock` writes into the *same* device-local store as
    `store_item` and is read by the same `get_item`; the write is delete-then-add
    because `SecItemUpdate` cannot change an existing item's protection class, and
    the class is the whole contract. The class is confined to notification material:
    it opens content, signs nothing, and is on the never-sync deny list.
    
    **The pinned sender-key set is keyed by hosting server.** `kid` is an
    autoincrement column on one instance, and two instances will both publish a
    `kid` of 1 for unrelated keys — which this wallet, holding identities on
    several hosts, would silently collapse into one entry. The extension will try
    every candidate under an incoming `kid`; HPKE Auth mode fails closed on a wrong
    sender key, so trying costs nothing.
    
    **A successful fetch replaces a host's set wholesale.** That single choice is
    what implements the design's rotation semantics: a key the operator revokes
    disappears from the device at its next contact. Merging would keep a compromised
    key pinned forever, which is the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close.
    A 501 or 503 changes nothing — neither is a revocation, and clearing on one
    would strip every device that checked in during a bad deploy.
    
    The APNs bridge is iOS-only and adds the two device-token delegate methods to
    Tauri's delegate class rather than swizzling: `class_addMethod` fails if the
    selector already exists, and declining is the outcome we want if Tauri ever
    implements them itself. Everything with logic worth testing lives in
    `notifications.rs` instead, since the bridge is only ever compiled by the
    cross-compile lane and only ever exercised on a device.
    
    Both apps move to iOS 17, where CryptoKit's HPKE API begins.
    
    Registration reports "no APNs token yet" and "this host runs no relay" as
    outcomes rather than errors, so the onboarding-completion call has nothing to
    catch on a simulator or for an identity hosted on a standard PDS.
    
    Not verified without a device: the delegate installation, the permission prompt,
    and that a real token round-trips. The iOS cross-compile is the only automated
    check those paths get.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Entire-Checkpoint: b5668e5ea8b5

content.content:
1	// pattern: Mixed (Functional Core pin-store arithmetic; Imperative Shell commands + Keychain)
2	//
3	// The device half of the end-to-end-encrypted notification relay: the keys a Custos instance
4	// seals push payloads to, the registration that tells it where to send them, and the pinned
5	// sender-key set the Notification Service Extension verifies against.
6	//
7	//   register_for_notifications(did)         — POST /v1/notifications/register
8	//   refresh_notification_sender_keys(did)   — GET  /v1/notifications/sender-keys (the re-pin)
9	//   get_notification_diagnostics()          — what this device holds, for Settings
10	//
11	// Nothing here decrypts anything. The extension that does is a separate target (a later phase);
12	// this module's whole job is to leave the right material in the right Keychain slots under the
13	// right protection class, and to keep the pinned set fresh.
14	//
15	// # Why the material is device-global rather than per-DID
16	//
17	// A push arrives at the extension as `{v, kid, enc, ct}` and nothing else — no DID, no handle,
18	// no account hint, because naming one would hand the relay and Apple the metadata the whole
19	// design exists to withhold. So the recipient key cannot be per-identity: the extension would
20	// have no way to choose among several. One device, one notification keypair, one `device_uuid`;
21	// every identity on the device registers the same public key with its own host.
22	//
23	// # Why the pinned set is per-host anyway
24	//
25	// `kid` is an autoincrement column on *one* Custos instance. Two instances will both publish a
26	// `kid` of 1 for entirely unrelated keys, and this wallet routinely holds identities on more
27	// than one. So the pin store is a map from hosting server to that server's published set, and
28	// the extension tries every candidate key registered under the incoming `kid`. That costs
29	// nothing and cannot go wrong: HPKE Auth mode either authenticates against a given sender key
30	// or it does not, so a wrong candidate fails closed and the next is tried. A single flat set
31	// keyed by `kid` alone would instead have two instances silently overwriting each other.
32	//
33	// # Re-pinning is wholesale replacement
34	//
35	// A successful fetch replaces that host's entry entirely rather than merging into it. That one
36	// choice is what implements all three rotation semantics from the design: a new key appears, a
37	// retired key stays as long as the server keeps publishing it, and a *revoked* key vanishes from
38	// this device the first time it contacts its Custos. Merging would keep a compromised key
39	// pinned forever, which is precisely the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close.
40	//
41	// A failed fetch changes nothing. An instance that answers 501 has not revoked anything — it has
42	// switched the feature off, or was never configured — and a 503 means it could not read its own
43	// keys. Treating either as "revoke everything" would let one bad deploy strip the pins off every
44	// device that happened to check in during it.
45	
46	use std::collections::BTreeMap;
47	
48	use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
49	use zeroize::Zeroizing;
50	
51	use crate::identity_store::IdentityStore;
52	use crate::oauth_client::OAuthClient;
53	use crate::pds_client::PdsClient;
54	use crate::session_provider::{SessionError, SessionProvider, UnlockReason};
55	
56	// ── Keychain accounts ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
57	
58	/// The device's stable notification identifier. App-generated and device-global: the server
59	/// keys registrations on `(did, device_uuid)` precisely because its own `devices` rows are
60	/// deleted at DID promotion, so this value must outlive every identity that uses it.
61	const DEVICE_UUID_ACCOUNT: &str = "notification-device-uuid";
62	
63	/// The per-device P-256 notification private key (raw 32-byte scalar).
64	///
65	/// `AccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, in the shared access group — the extension decrypts on a locked
66	/// screen and cannot present a biometric prompt. The relaxation is bounded: this key opens
67	/// notification *content* and signs nothing. It is not a rotation key, not a repo signing key,
68	/// and its loss costs unreadable banners, never an identity.
69	const NOTIFICATION_KEY_ACCOUNT: &str = "notification-key-priv";
70	
71	/// The pinned sender-key sets, one per hosting server. Same protection class as the private
72	/// key: the extension needs both in the same moment, and a key it cannot read is a payload it
73	/// must render as unverified.
74	const PINNED_SENDER_KEYS_ACCOUNT: &str = "notification-sender-keys";
75	
76	/// The APNs device token, lowercase hex. Ordinary protection — only the foreground app reads it,
77	/// to put it in a registration request.
78	const APNS_TOKEN_ACCOUNT: &str = "notification-apns-token";
79	
80	/// Every account this module owns, so `keychain.rs`'s never-sync assertion is written against
81	/// the list rather than a copy of it — a new slot added here is covered without anyone
82	/// remembering to go and add it there too.
83	#[cfg(test)]
84	pub(crate) const NOTIFICATION_ACCOUNTS: &[&str] = &[
85	    DEVICE_UUID_ACCOUNT,
86	    NOTIFICATION_KEY_ACCOUNT,
87	    PINNED_SENDER_KEYS_ACCOUNT,
88	    APNS_TOKEN_ACCOUNT,
89	];
90	
91	/// Version tag on the stored pin document, so a later shape change can be recognized rather
92	/// than mis-parsed.
93	const PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION: u8 = 1;
94	
95	// ── Errors ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
96	
97	/// Errors from the notification commands.
98	///
99	/// Serializes as `{ "code": "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE", ... }`, matching the sibling wallet error
100	/// enums. Note what is deliberately *absent*: there is no error for "this device has no APNs
101	/// token yet" or "this host does not do notifications". Both are ordinary states — a simulator
102	/// has no token, a claimed identity on bsky.social will never have a relay — and the commands
103	/// report them as outcomes, so onboarding has nothing to catch.
104	#[derive(Debug, Serialize, thiserror::Error)]
105	#[serde(
106	    tag = "code",
107	    rename_all = "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE",
108	    rename_all_fields = "camelCase"
109	)]
110	pub enum NotificationsError {
111	    /// The identity's session could not be resolved without an unlock — the frontend's cue to
112	    /// run `unlockIdentity(did)` and retry.
113	    #[error("identity is locked and needs an unlock")]
114	    SessionLocked { reason: UnlockReason },
115	    /// The hosting PDS rate limited the request.
116	    #[error("rate limited")]
117	    RateLimited { retry_after: Option<String> },
118	    /// The DID is not registered in this wallet.
119	    #[error("identity not found: {message}")]
120	    IdentityNotFound { message: String },
121	    /// A notification key could not be generated.
122	    #[error("could not generate the notification key: {message}")]
123	    KeyGenerationFailed { message: String },
124	    /// The Keychain refused a read or a write.
125	    #[error("keychain error: {message}")]
126	    KeychainError { message: String },
127	    /// The hosting server refused for a non-connectivity reason. `status` is the HTTP code where
128	    /// there was one, and `None` for a session-lifecycle verdict that is not a transport failure.
129	    #[error("server error: {message}")]
130	    ServerError {
131	        status: Option<u16>,
132	        message: String,
133	    },
134	    /// A network / transport call failed.
135	    #[error("network error: {message}")]
136	    NetworkError { message: String },
137	}
138	
139	/// Map a session-lifecycle failure onto this surface. Exhaustive on purpose: only a genuine
140	/// transport failure becomes `NetworkError`, so a server verdict or a Keychain fault is never
141	/// mislabelled "check your connection" (the same discipline as `app_passwords.rs`).
142	fn map_session_error(error: SessionError) -> NotificationsError {
143	    match error {
144	        SessionError::NeedsUnlock { reason } => NotificationsError::SessionLocked { reason },
145	        SessionError::RateLimited { retry_after } => {
146	            NotificationsError::RateLimited { retry_after }
147	        }
148	        SessionError::IdentityNotFound => NotificationsError::IdentityNotFound {
149	            message: "identity not found".to_string(),
150	        },
151	        SessionError::Offline { message } => NotificationsError::NetworkError { message },
152	        SessionError::ServerFailure { status } => NotificationsError::ServerError {
153	            status: Some(status),
154	            message: format!("session request failed with status {status}"),
155	        },
156	        SessionError::UnsupportedHost => NotificationsError::ServerError {
157	            status: None,
158	            message: "the identity's hosting server does not support session refresh".to_string(),
159	        },
160	        SessionError::Keychain { message } => NotificationsError::KeychainError { message },
161	        SessionError::InvalidResponse { message } => NotificationsError::ServerError {
162	            status: None,
163	            message: format!("invalid session response: {message}"),
164	        },
165	    }
166	}
167	
168	fn keychain_err(e: crate::keychain::KeychainError) -> NotificationsError {
169	    NotificationsError::KeychainError {
170	        message: e.to_string(),
171	    }
172	}
173	
174	// ── Wire + storage types ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
175	
176	/// One published sender key. Mirrors the server's `sender-keys` element exactly, so the
177	/// response deserializes straight into what gets pinned.
178	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
179	#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
180	pub struct SenderKey {
181	    /// The instance-scoped key id a sealed payload's envelope names.
182	    pub kid: i64,
183	    /// The P-256 `did:key` to verify the seal against.
184	    pub public_key: String,
185	}
186	
187	#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
188	struct SenderKeysResponse {
189	    keys: Vec<SenderKey>,
190	}
191	
192	#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
193	#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
194	struct RegisterRequest<'a> {
195	    device_uuid: &'a str,
196	    notification_public_key: &'a str,
197	    apns_token: &'a str,
198	    apns_topic: &'a str,
199	}
200	
201	/// The whole pin store: every hosting server this device has re-pinned against.
202	///
203	/// Read **fail-open** — an unreadable document is treated as empty. That is the opposite of
204	/// `ceremony-staging`'s fail-closed contract, and for the opposite reason: this holds public
205	/// keys the server will hand back on the next contact, so refusing to proceed would forfeit the
206	/// re-pin that repairs it in order to protect a copy of something already recoverable.
207	#[derive(Debug, Default, Serialize, Deserialize)]
208	struct PinnedSenderKeys {
209	    version: u8,
210	    /// Hosting server (normalized by [`host_key`]) → that server's published set.
211	    hosts: BTreeMap<String, Vec<SenderKey>>,
212	}
213	
214	/// Normalize a PDS base URL into a pin-store key, so `https://Pds.Example.com/` and
215	/// `https://pds.example.com` are one host. Same rule as `pds_capabilities`' cache key; kept
216	/// separate because that one is a process cache and this one is written to disk.
217	fn host_key(pds_url: &str) -> String {
218	    pds_url.trim().trim_end_matches('/').to_ascii_lowercase()
219	}
220	
221	// ── Command results ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
222	
223	/// What a registration attempt actually did.
224	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize)]
225	#[serde(rename_all = "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE")]
226	pub enum RegistrationStatus {
227	    /// The server stored the registration and is minting a relay handle for it.
228	    Registered,
229	    /// This device has no APNs token yet: the simulator never issues one, the user may not have
230	    /// granted permission, and even on a granted device the token arrives asynchronously after
231	    /// launch. Not a failure — the token-change callback re-registers when one shows up.
232	    AwaitingApnsToken,
233	    /// The identity's host serves no notification routes (it answered 501). A standard PDS
234	    /// always will, and so will a Custos whose operator configured no relay.
235	    Unsupported,
236	}
237	
238	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)]
239	#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
240	pub struct RegistrationOutcome {
241	    pub status: RegistrationStatus,
242	    /// The stable identifier this device registered under, echoed so the UI and the diagnostics
243	    /// export name the same thing the server row is keyed by.
244	    pub device_uuid: String,
245	    /// The device's notification `did:key`, or `None` when the attempt stopped before a key was
246	    /// needed.
247	    pub notification_key_id: Option<String>,
248	}

278	/// The device's stable notification identifier, generated on first use.
279	///
280	/// Idempotent: every later call returns the same value, because the server's registration row is
281	/// keyed by it and a fresh one on each launch would accumulate a dead row (and a live relay
282	/// handle) per app start.
283	pub fn device_uuid() -> Result<String, NotificationsError> {
284	    match crate::keychain::get_item(DEVICE_UUID_ACCOUNT) {
285	        Ok(bytes) => {
286	            if let Ok(existing) = String::from_utf8(bytes) {
287	                if !existing.is_empty() {
288	                    return Ok(existing);
289	                }
290	            }
291	            // An unreadable identifier is not recoverable and not secret: mint a new one rather
292	            // than wedging registration forever. The stale server row ages out with the relay's
293	            // handle when APNs reports the token gone.
294	            tracing::warn!("notification device uuid is unreadable; minting a replacement");
295	            mint_device_uuid()
296	        }
297	        Err(e) if crate::keychain::is_not_found(&e) => mint_device_uuid(),
298	        Err(e) => Err(keychain_err(e)),
299	    }
300	}
301	
302	/// Mint the device's identifier, **verifying it read back** before reporting it.
303	///
304	/// The same discipline the notification key and every Share 1 writer use, and for a sharper
305	/// reason here: a write that reports success without persisting is indistinguishable from never
306	/// having run, so the next launch mints another identifier and registers again — accumulating
307	/// exactly the dead row and live relay handle per app start that [`device_uuid`] exists to
308	/// prevent. Failing loudly costs one registration attempt; succeeding quietly costs one forever.
309	fn mint_device_uuid() -> Result<String, NotificationsError> {
310	    let uuid = uuid::Uuid::new_v4().to_string();
311	    crate::keychain::store_item(DEVICE_UUID_ACCOUNT, uuid.as_bytes()).map_err(keychain_err)?;
312	    match crate::keychain::get_item(DEVICE_UUID_ACCOUNT) {
313	        Ok(bytes) if bytes == uuid.as_bytes() => Ok(uuid),
314	        _ => Err(NotificationsError::KeychainError {
315	            message: "the device uuid did not read back after storing".to_string(),
316	        }),
317	    }
318	}
319	
320	/// Load — or, on first use, generate — the device's notification keypair, returning its
321	/// `did:key`.
322	///
323	/// The private scalar is written under `AccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` and **read back before the
324	/// key is reported**, the same discipline every Share 1 writer uses. Here the failure it guards
325	/// is quiet by construction: a key the app believes it stored but the extension cannot find
326	/// turns every future notification into the unverified notice, with nothing anywhere saying why.
327	fn load_or_create_notification_key() -> Result<String, NotificationsError> {
328	    if let Some(scalar) = stored_notification_scalar()? {
329	        match crypto::p256_keypair_from_secret(&scalar) {
330	            Ok(keypair) => return Ok(keypair.key_id.0),
331	            // A stored 32-byte value that is not a valid scalar (zero, or past the curve order)
332	            // gets the same verdict as a wrong-length one: unreconstructable either way. Erroring
333	            // instead would refuse every future registration forever, since nothing else ever
334	            // overwrites this slot — and the only thing minting costs is payloads already sealed
335	            // to a key nobody can rebuild.
336	            Err(e) => tracing::warn!(
337	                error = %e,
338	                "stored notification key is unusable; minting a replacement"
339	            ),
340	        }
341	    }
342	
343	    let keypair =
344	        crypto::generate_p256_keypair().map_err(|e| NotificationsError::KeyGenerationFailed {
345	            message: e.to_string(),
346	        })?;
347	    crate::keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock(
348	        NOTIFICATION_KEY_ACCOUNT,
349	        keypair.private_key_bytes.as_ref(),
350	    )
351	    .map_err(keychain_err)?;
352	
353	    match stored_notification_scalar()? {
354	        Some(read_back) if read_back.as_ref() == keypair.private_key_bytes.as_ref() => {
355	            Ok(keypair.key_id.0)
356	        }
357	        _ => Err(NotificationsError::KeychainError {
358	            message: "the notification key did not read back after storing".to_string(),
359	        }),
360	    }
361	}
362	
363	/// The stored notification private scalar, or `None` when none is stored.
364	///
365	/// A stored value of the wrong length is treated as absent so the caller mints a fresh key: the
366	/// only thing lost is the ability to open payloads sealed to a key nobody can reconstruct
367	/// anyway.
368	fn stored_notification_scalar() -> Result<Option<Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>>, NotificationsError> {
369	    match crate::keychain::get_item(NOTIFICATION_KEY_ACCOUNT) {
370	        Ok(bytes) if bytes.len() == 32 => {
371	            let mut scalar = [0u8; 32];
372	            scalar.copy_from_slice(&bytes);
373	            Ok(Some(Zeroizing::new(scalar)))
374	        }
375	        Ok(_) => {
376	            tracing::warn!("notification key has an unexpected length; treating it as absent");
377	            Ok(None)
378	        }
379	        Err(e) if crate::keychain::is_not_found(&e) => Ok(None),
380	        Err(e) => Err(keychain_err(e)),
381	    }
382	}

386	/// Record the APNs device token iOS handed us, reporting whether it actually changed.
387	///
388	/// Gated to iOS and tests because the only production caller is `apns.rs`, which iOS alone
389	/// compiles — the same shape `bg_backup.rs` uses for its scheduling payload.
390	///
391	/// `false` means the token is the one already stored, which is the common case: iOS delivers a
392	/// token on every launch, and re-registering every identity each time would spend a round trip
393	/// per identity per launch to write rows that already say this.
394	#[cfg(any(target_os = "ios", test))]
395	pub(crate) fn record_apns_token(token: &str) -> Result<bool, NotificationsError> {
396	    let token = token.to_ascii_lowercase();

398	        return Ok(false);
399	    }
400	    crate::keychain::store_item(APNS_TOKEN_ACCOUNT, token.as_bytes()).map_err(keychain_err)?;
401	    Ok(true)
402	}

429	/// The pin store as it currently stands. Never fails: an unreadable document reads as empty
430	/// (see [`PinnedSenderKeys`]).
431	fn load_pins() -> PinnedSenderKeys {
432	    let raw = match crate::keychain::get_item(PINNED_SENDER_KEYS_ACCOUNT) {
433	        Ok(bytes) => bytes,
434	        Err(e) => {
435	            if !crate::keychain::is_not_found(&e) {
436	                tracing::warn!(error = %e, "could not read pinned sender keys; treating as empty");
437	            }
438	            return PinnedSenderKeys {
439	                version: PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION,
440	                hosts: BTreeMap::new(),
441	            };
442	        }
443	    };
444	    match serde_json::from_slice::<PinnedSenderKeys>(&raw) {
445	        Ok(pins) if pins.version == PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION => pins,
446	        Ok(pins) => {
447	            tracing::warn!(
448	                version = pins.version,
449	                "pinned sender keys were written by a different build; re-pinning from scratch"
450	            );
451	            PinnedSenderKeys {
452	                version: PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION,
453	                hosts: BTreeMap::new(),
454	            }
455	        }
456	        Err(e) => {
457	            tracing::warn!(error = %e, "pinned sender keys are corrupt; re-pinning from scratch");
458	            PinnedSenderKeys {
459	                version: PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION,
460	                hosts: BTreeMap::new(),
461	            }
462	        }
463	    }
464	}

466	/// Replace one host's pinned set, leaving every other host untouched.
467	///
468	/// Wholesale for the named host — that is the revocation mechanism — and surgical across hosts,
469	/// because a contact with one identity's Custos says nothing about another's.
470	/// One shared document means one writer at a time.
471	///
472	/// `+page.svelte` fires a registration per identity **without awaiting**, and each one re-pins on
473	/// the same contact, so two of these read-modify-writes genuinely overlap on Tauri's multi-thread
474	/// runtime. Losing the later write is not merely a stale entry: if the discarded pass was the
475	/// contact that dropped a *revoked* sender key, that host keeps trusting the revoked key until
476	/// its next contact — reopening the exact window the module header says re-pinning closes.
477	///
478	/// A `std::sync::Mutex` deliberately: the guard is taken and released entirely inside this
479	/// synchronous function and never crosses an `.await`.
480	static PIN_WRITE_LOCK: std::sync::Mutex<()> = std::sync::Mutex::new(());
481	
482	fn store_pins_for_host(host: &str, keys: &[SenderKey]) -> Result<(), NotificationsError> {
483	    // A poisoned lock means some other thread panicked mid-write; the document is re-read below
484	    // either way, so recovering is strictly better than propagating the panic into a re-pin.
485	    let _guard = PIN_WRITE_LOCK.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
486	    let mut pins = load_pins();
487	    pins.version = PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION;
488	    pins.hosts.insert(host.to_string(), keys.to_vec());
489	
490	    let encoded = serde_json::to_vec(&pins).map_err(|e| NotificationsError::KeychainError {
491	        message: format!("could not encode pinned sender keys: {e}"),
492	    })?;
493	    crate::keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock(PINNED_SENDER_KEYS_ACCOUNT, &encoded)
494	        .map_err(keychain_err)
495	}

499	fn oauth_err(e: crate::oauth::OAuthError) -> NotificationsError {
500	    NotificationsError::NetworkError {
501	        message: e.to_string(),
502	    }
503	}

505	/// `POST /v1/notifications/register`. `Ok(false)` is the host's 501 — it serves no notification
506	/// routes — which the caller reports as `Unsupported` rather than an error.
507	async fn register_impl(
508	    client: &OAuthClient,
509	    request: &RegisterRequest<'_>,
510	) -> Result<bool, NotificationsError> {
511	    let resp = client
512	        .post("/v1/notifications/register", request)
513	        .await
514	        .map_err(oauth_err)?;
515	    match resp.status().as_u16() {
516	        200 => Ok(true),
517	        501 => Ok(false),
518	        429 => Err(NotificationsError::RateLimited {
519	            retry_after: resp
520	                .headers()
521	                .get("retry-after")
522	                .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
523	                .map(str::to_string),
524	        }),
525	        other => Err(NotificationsError::ServerError {
526	            status: Some(other),
527	            message: server_message(resp, "registration was refused").await,
528	        }),
529	    }
530	}
531	
532	/// `GET /v1/notifications/sender-keys`. `Ok(None)` is the 501; every other non-200 is an error,
533	/// including the 503 an instance returns when it cannot read its own keys — pinning nothing on
534	/// that basis would leave the device silently unable to verify anything it later receives.
535	async fn fetch_sender_keys_impl(
536	    client: &OAuthClient,
537	) -> Result<Option<Vec<SenderKey>>, NotificationsError> {
538	    let resp = client
539	        .get("/v1/notifications/sender-keys")
540	        .await
541	        .map_err(oauth_err)?;
542	    match resp.status().as_u16() {
543	        200 => {
544	            let body: SenderKeysResponse =
545	                resp.json()
546	                    .await
547	                    .map_err(|e| NotificationsError::ServerError {
548	                        status: Some(200),
549	                        message: format!("could not parse the sender-key set: {e}"),
550	                    })?;
551	            Ok(Some(body.keys))
552	        }
553	        501 => Ok(None),
554	        429 => Err(NotificationsError::RateLimited {
555	            retry_after: resp
556	                .headers()
557	                .get("retry-after")
558	                .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
559	                .map(str::to_string),
560	        }),
561	        other => Err(NotificationsError::ServerError {
562	            status: Some(other),
563	            message: server_message(resp, "the sender-key set is unavailable").await,
564	        }),
565	    }
566	}

568	/// The server's own error message where it sent one, so the screen shows the real reason instead
569	/// of a status code.
570	async fn server_message(resp: reqwest::Response, fallback: &str) -> String {
571	    #[derive(Deserialize)]
572	    struct Envelope {
573	        error: Option<Inner>,
574	    }
575	    #[derive(Deserialize)]
576	    struct Inner {
577	        message: Option<String>,
578	    }
579	    resp.json::<Envelope>()
580	        .await
581	        .ok()
582	        .and_then(|e| e.error)
583	        .and_then(|e| e.message)
584	        .unwrap_or_else(|| fallback.to_string())
585	}

587	/// Resolve the DID's full-access session (restore / refresh, or `SessionLocked`).
588	async fn full_access_session(
589	    pds_client: &PdsClient,
590	    did: &str,
591	) -> Result<crate::session_provider::ActiveSession, NotificationsError> {
592	    // Not `NetworkError`: an unreadable clock is a local fault, and this module's rule is that
593	    // only a transport failure may be reported as one — otherwise the screen offers connectivity
594	    // advice for a problem connectivity cannot fix.
595	    let now = crate::sovereign_session::unix_timestamp().map_err(|_| {
596	        NotificationsError::ServerError {
597	            status: None,
598	            message: "system clock is unavailable".to_string(),
599	        }
600	    })?;
601	    SessionProvider
602	        .full_access_client(pds_client, &IdentityStore, did, now)
603	        .await
604	        .map_err(map_session_error)
605	}

609	/// Tauri command: register this device for push on the identity's hosting Custos.
610	///
611	/// Called at onboarding completion (post-promotion, so the account exists and can be
612	/// authenticated) and again whenever the APNs token changes. Idempotent on the server, which
613	/// upserts on `(did, device_uuid)`, so a repeat is free — which is what lets the caller fire it
614	/// without tracking whether it already has.
615	#[tauri::command]
616	pub async fn register_for_notifications(
617	    app: tauri::AppHandle,
618	    state: tauri::State<'_, crate::oauth::AppState>,
619	    did: String,
620	) -> Result<RegistrationOutcome, NotificationsError> {
621	    // The topic is the app's own bundle identifier, read from the running configuration rather
622	    // than restated as a constant here — APNs routes on the identifier the binary was actually
623	    // built with, and a rename that missed a hardcoded copy would fail at the relay, one hop
624	    // away from anything that could explain it.
625	    register_identity(&app.config().identifier, state.pds_client(), &did).await
626	}
627	
628	/// Register one identity, given the APNs topic and a PDS client.
629	///
630	/// Split out from the command because the APNs token-change callback re-registers every managed
631	/// identity from a context that has no Tauri `State` — and a second implementation of the same
632	/// sequence is exactly how the two would drift.
633	pub(crate) async fn register_identity(
634	    apns_topic: &str,
635	    pds_client: &PdsClient,
636	    did: &str,
637	) -> Result<RegistrationOutcome, NotificationsError> {
638	    let device_uuid = device_uuid()?;
639	
640	    // Checked before the key is generated or the session resolved: with no token there is
641	    // nothing to register, and minting key material for a registration that cannot happen would
642	    // pin this device to a key its host has never heard of.
643	    let Some(apns_token) = stored_apns_token() else {
644	        return Ok(RegistrationOutcome {
645	            status: RegistrationStatus::AwaitingApnsToken,
646	            device_uuid,
647	            notification_key_id: None,
648	        });
649	    };
650	
651	    let notification_key_id = load_or_create_notification_key()?;
652	    let session = full_access_session(pds_client, did).await?;
653	
654	    let registered = register_impl(
655	        &session.client,
656	        &RegisterRequest {
657	            device_uuid: &device_uuid,
658	            notification_public_key: &notification_key_id,
659	            apns_token: &apns_token,
660	            apns_topic,
661	        },
662	    )
663	    .await?;
664	
665	    // The same contact re-pins. The registration is the first moment this device could receive
666	    // anything from this host, so it is also the first moment it needs the keys to verify it.
667	    if registered {
668	        if let Err(e) = pin_sender_keys(&session.client, &session.pds_url).await {
669	            tracing::warn!(error = ?e, "registered for push but could not pin sender keys");
670	        }
671	    }
672	
673	    Ok(RegistrationOutcome {
674	        status: if registered {
675	            RegistrationStatus::Registered
676	        } else {
677	            RegistrationStatus::Unsupported
678	        },
679	        device_uuid,
680	        notification_key_id: Some(notification_key_id),
681	    })
682	}

684	/// Re-register every managed identity, after the APNs token changed under us.
685	///
686	/// Per identity rather than once: the registration lives on each identity's own hosting Custos,
687	/// which may be a different server (or no Custos at all). Failures are logged and stepped over —
688	/// one identity whose host is unreachable must not cost the others their new token, and the next
689	/// contact retries anyway.
690	#[cfg(target_os = "ios")]
691	pub(crate) async fn re_register_every_identity(apns_topic: &str, pds_client: &PdsClient) {
692	    let dids = match IdentityStore.list_identities() {
693	        Ok(dids) => dids,
694	        Err(e) => {
695	            tracing::warn!(error = ?e, "could not list identities to re-register for push");
696	            return;
697	        }
698	    };
699	    for did in dids {
700	        match register_identity(apns_topic, pds_client, &did).await {
701	            Ok(outcome) => {
702	                tracing::info!(did = %did, status = ?outcome.status, "re-registered for push")
703	            }
704	            Err(e) => tracing::warn!(did = %did, error = ?e, "could not re-register for push"),
705	        }
706	    }
707	}

709	/// Tauri command: re-fetch and re-pin the identity's host's sender-key set.
710	///
711	/// The frontend calls this on every successful contact with a Custos. That cadence is the
712	/// design's compromise-window property, not housekeeping: a sender key the operator revokes
713	/// stops being trusted on this device at the next contact, and nothing shorter than that is
714	/// available without a channel the relay could interfere with.
715	#[tauri::command]
716	pub async fn refresh_notification_sender_keys(
717	    state: tauri::State<'_, crate::oauth::AppState>,
718	    did: String,
719	) -> Result<SenderKeyPinning, NotificationsError> {
720	    let session = full_access_session(state.pds_client(), &did).await?;
721	    pin_sender_keys(&session.client, &session.pds_url).await
722	}

724	/// Fetch and store one host's set. Shared by the re-pin command and the registration path.
725	async fn pin_sender_keys(
726	    client: &OAuthClient,
727	    pds_url: &str,
728	) -> Result<SenderKeyPinning, NotificationsError> {
729	    let host = host_key(pds_url);
730	    match fetch_sender_keys_impl(client).await? {
731	        Some(keys) => {
732	            store_pins_for_host(&host, &keys)?;
733	            Ok(SenderKeyPinning {
734	                host,
735	                pinned: true,
736	                keys,
737	            })
738	        }
739	        None => {
740	            let keys = load_pins().hosts.get(&host).cloned().unwrap_or_default();
741	            Ok(SenderKeyPinning {
742	                host,
743	                pinned: false,
744	                keys,
745	            })
746	        }
747	    }
748	}

751	/// the Settings answer to "why am I not getting notifications", and it must work in exactly the
752	/// states where nothing else does.
753	#[tauri::command]
754	pub fn get_notification_diagnostics() -> NotificationDiagnostics {
755	    NotificationDiagnostics {
756	        device_uuid: crate::keychain::get_item(DEVICE_UUID_ACCOUNT)
757	            .ok()
758	            .and_then(|b| String::from_utf8(b).ok())

761	            .ok()

763	            .and_then(|scalar| crypto::p256_keypair_from_secret(&scalar).ok())
764	            .map(|keypair| keypair.key_id.0),
765	        has_apns_token: stored_apns_token().is_some(),
766	        pinned_hosts: load_pins().hosts,
767	    }

# Obsign (identity-wallet) Mobile App

Last verified: 2026-07-08
Last updated: 2026-07-27

## Purpose

Tauri v2 iOS application — SvelteKit 2 + Svelte 5 frontend running in a native WKWebView, communicating with a Rust backend exclusively through Tauri's IPC bridge.

## Browser test harness (drive the app without a simulator)

The whole frontend runs in a plain desktop browser under `vite dev` — the only thing the
browser lacks is the Tauri `invoke()` seam, which the harness intercepts with Tauri's
official `mockIPC`. This lets an agent (or a human) reach every screen and reproduce any
state, including rare error states, without a Mac/Xcode/simulator. Design + acceptance
criteria: [docs/archive/design-plans/2026-07-12-browser-harness.md](../../docs/archive/design-plans/2026-07-12-browser-harness.md).

**Start it** (or use the `.claude/launch.json` config `wallet-harness` / `wallet-harness-proxy`):
- **Fake mode** (default, no backend needed): `pnpm --dir apps/identity-wallet dev:harness` → http://localhost:5173.
- **Proxy mode** (real thin-HTTP calls against a hermetic local PDS): in one terminal
  `cargo build -p pds` then `just harness-pds` (prints the URL + admin token); in another,
  `VITE_HARNESS_PDS_URL=<url> VITE_HARNESS_ADMIN_TOKEN=<token> pnpm --dir apps/identity-wallet dev:harness:proxy`.
- Plain `pnpm dev` never activates the harness (double-gated on `import.meta.env.DEV && VITE_HARNESS`);
  `pnpm check:harness-absence` proves it is tree-shaken out of production builds.

**`window.__harness` console API** (both modes):
- `.scenario(name)` — switch preset and reload (persists across reload). Presets:
  `fresh-install`, `foreign-pds` (a spec-compliant non-Custos host — advertises no
  capabilities, so the create flow's gate closes and steers to import),
  `unreachable-pds` (the same empty capability list, but `reached: false` — the gate must
  show a retryable error, never the steer), `one-identity`, `multi-identity`,
  `alert-active`, plus its three siblings covering the rest of the recovery-window
  urgency ladder — `alert-warning` (~12h left), `alert-critical` (~3h left) and
  `alert-expired` (past the window, the only way to reach `AlertDetailScreen`'s
  disabled "Recovery window expired" button); the four differ only in how old the
  seeded change is, since that is what `getUrgency` reads. `alert-multi` seeds TWO alarmed
  identities at different ages — the only preset that reaches the multi-identity half of the
  launch takeover (which lands on Protection rather than on one identity's alarm surface)
  and Protection's "Not now" exit. `device-key-unusable` (a device restored from an encrypted backup: the
  device-key metadata came back, the Secure Enclave key did not — the only way to reach the
  "can no longer sign" degraded state in a browser with no enclave), `migration-in-flight`,
  `agent-connected`, `app-password-minted`, plus the share-recovery matrix:
  `recover-escrow` (happy path A — iCloud Share 1 + zero-delay escrow release),
  `recover-sovereign` (happy path B — manual Share 3 entry; paste
  `state().recovery.fixtures.share3Words` or `.share3`), `recover-wrong-set`
  (`fixtures.wrongSet` → SHARE_SET_MISMATCH), `recover-corrupt-share`
  (`fixtures.corrupt` → SHARE_CHECKSUM), `recover-mismatch` (verification fails —
  shares don't match the identity), `recover-pending-delay` (24h escrow window; the
  second poll releases), `recover-cancelled` (pending release cancelled → uniform
  401 on poll), `recover-epilogue-resume` (launch resumes an interrupted rotation
  epilogue); plus the escrow-less kit pair: `self-held-kit` (a claimed identity on a
  non-Custos host — device key at `rotationKeys[0]`, a longer claimed tail than the
  re-key's `[device, PDS]`, no recovery key, host advertises nothing) and
  `self-held-kit-escrow-host` (the same identity after the kit, now hosted somewhere that
  DOES advertise `escrow` — the upsell seam's only true state). `.scenarios` lists them.
- `.failNext(command, error)` — make the next call of `command` reject with a typed error,
  e.g. `window.__harness.failNext('create_account', { code: 'EXPIRED_CODE' })`.
- `.emit(event, payload)` — deliver a Tauri event to live `listen()` subscribers;
  `window.__harness.emit('auth_ready')` simulates the OAuth deep-link return.
- `.state()` — a read-only snapshot of the fake store. `.mode` is `'fake'` or `'proxy'`.

**Proxy mode is real only for the thin-HTTP subset** — `create_account` (mints + redeems a
real claim code, POSTs `/v1/accounts/mobile`) and `get_available_user_domains`
(describeServer). By the honest boundary, these stay **faked even in proxy mode** (heavy
Rust logic with no thin-HTTP form): the DID ceremony (`perform_did_ceremony`,
`*_did_web_ceremony`), OAuth completion (`prepare/complete_oauth_flow`), the migration
transfer legs (`transfer_repo`/`transfer_blobs`/…, `finalize_migration`), recovery/claim
PLC ops, and the agent surfaces (which need a real post-ceremony session the faked
ceremony never mints). Fidelity the browser can never cover: real Keychain/Secure-Enclave,
the biometric prompt, ASWebAuthenticationSession, WKWebView rendering, safe-area insets,
camera/QR — those stay simulator/device concerns.

**Fake handler coverage is enforced:** every command in `$lib/ipc` must have a handler in
`src/lib/harness/registry.ts` or `registry.test.ts` fails (`pnpm test`). Harness code lives
in `src/lib/harness/` (`install`/`registry`/`state`/`scenarios`/`control` + `proxy/`),
activated by `src/hooks.client.ts`.

The vestibule is **additive framing only** — every operation keeps its own biometric gate, pre-sign review, and hold-to-confirm. SecurityCheckup is the quiet disclosure hanging off a secure StatusPanel (key custody, public-record watch, media + posts backup freshness), all reads of state the wallet already holds. ChangeHandleScreen is the sovereign change-handle surface reached from ManageIdentityScreen's "Change handle" row (did:plc + device-key-as-root only): it loads the hosting PDS's served domains, pre-flights the session (`ensureIdentitySession`, `unlockIdentity` on `NEEDS_UNLOCK`), then runs the biometric-gated `changeHandle`. AppPasswordsScreen is the app-password surface reached from the identity screen's Use zone ("Sign in to Bluesky"): it lists/mints/revokes the account's scoped app passwords via `SessionProvider::full_access_client` (SESSION_LOCKED → `unlockIdentity` + retry ($lib/unlock: sovereign login on a Custos host, password prompt elsewhere); mint and revoke are biometric-gated; the generated secret is shown once with copy and never persisted). MediaBackupScreen is the user-held blob-backup surface reached from ManageIdentityScreen's "Backups" row (media and posts are presented as one item because they are one job): opt-in with the mirror size always shown, "Back up now" (incremental, CID-verified sync pass over public sync endpoints — no session), and a biometric-gated "Restore to server" (`uploadBlob` via `SessionProvider::full_access_client`; SESSION_LOCKED → `unlockIdentity` + retry ($lib/unlock: sovereign login on a Custos host, password prompt elsewhere)), with per-blob failures listed rather than aborting the run. The same screen also holds a "Back up your posts" section (`repo_backup.rs`): opt-in with the snapshot size + last-backup shown, and "Back up posts now" (a full-CAR `getRepo` snapshot, validated client-side before it replaces the prior copy — no session, no biometric); there is no repo "restore" button (an `importRepo` needs a deactivated account, so restore flows through migration). `+page.svelte` fires silent opportunistic `runBlobBackup` **and** `runRepoBackup` passes on app open for opted-in identities (each on its own per-DID flag). MyAgentsScreen is the agent list; AgentDetailScreen is the per-agent sub-view (audit-trail paging + biometric-gated revoke) it renders on selection, its lifetime scoped to that selection. RemoveIdentityScreen is the permanent-removal flow (warn → emailed-code (+ password) → biometric-gated hold-to-remove → progress, with a "tombstone pending, retry" state), reached from AdvancedToolsScreen's destructive `onremove` (behind the vestibule). The password field is shown only when `getIdentityRemovalRoute` says the identity's host needs it: where the host advertises `walletAccountDelete` the wallet signs a device-key removal proof instead, so the confirm step is the code alone — an identity created without a password has nothing to type there, and the warning copy stays silent about a credential until the route resolves rather than promising one it may drop. Offered for **both** DID methods, with the screen branching on `did:web:` throughout: the warning drops the "retire on the network by tombstoning" promise (a did:web has no tombstone), the escape hatch's advanced "also retire on the network" option is withheld (it could not do what it says), and a successful removal ends in the `web_epilogue` state rather than returning to the identity list — the DID keeps resolving until its `did.json` leaves the domain, which only whoever controls that domain can do. The screen switches on the outcome's `tombstoneCid` being null (the backend's honest report that no tombstone was published), not on the DID string alone

- `src/routes/+page.svelte` — root page: three-flow state machine starting at `add_identity` (`AddIdentityScreen` — **one situation question**, "Add an identity — what's your situation?", replacing the old create/import/recover door taxonomy: `onfresh` opens `identity_method`, `IdentityMethodScreen` — the did:plc / did:web method fork; `onexisting` opens `identity_input`; `onlostwallet` opens `recover_start`; `onservergone` opens `server_gone`). **Create flow:** add_identity -> `identity_method` -> [did:plc: pds_config; new did:web: `did_web_path` -> `did_web_domain` -> pds_config] -> claim_code -> email -> handle -> password (every pre-submit step wires `onback` to the previous step) -> loading -> did_ceremony (the did:web branch runs `did_web_ceremony` instead) -> did_success -> shamir_backup -> handle_registration -> complete -> home (after handle_registration succeeds, `finishCreateFlow()` calls `registerCreatedIdentity()` to persist the new identity to `IdentityStore` so it appears in `IdentityListHome` — best-effort, never blocks the flow). `complete` goes **straight to `home`**: there is no post-create OAuth round trip and no browser hand-off (see the Key Decision below). `pds_config` is a **capability gate**, not just a form: after `savePdsUrl` (which re-probes the host, so this reads a warm cache) it calls `getPdsCapabilities()` and, unless the host advertises `createCeremony`, routes to `create_unavailable` (`CreateUnavailableScreen`) instead of `claim_code` — the create ceremony is Custos-structural, so a standard PDS is refused before the user types an account detail rather than failing inside `/v1/accounts/mobile`. This is the one gate that reads `ServerCapabilities.reached`: it does not merely withhold a feature, it tells the user their server cannot create identities, and a host that could not be asked must produce a retryable error instead of that accusation. The gate covers both create paths, since the did:web branch also passes through `pds_config`. From `create_unavailable` the import flow is one tap away with the chosen server still configured. **Import flow:** add_identity -> identity_input -> pds_auth -> email_verification -> review_operation -> claim_success -> home. **Existing did:web** takes the third `identity_method` branch: `did_web_path` (choose "existing") -> `did_web_existing`, which calls `importDidWebIdentity()` to bring the live document under wallet management, then enters the method-agnostic outbound-migration flow at `migration_start` (a did:web has no claim ceremony — control is proven by the domain publish and the source-PDS password, not a PLC op). **Home:** home -> { protection (the app-level Defend surface, from the protection strip) | identity_detail (the instrument panel) -> { move_or_rebuild -> { migration_start | recovery_rebuild_start } | manage_identity -> { change_handle | media_backup | did_document | advanced_tools -> { self_held_kit_review | rotate_repo_key | endpoint_repair | remove_identity } } | app_passwords | my_agents | oauth_consent_approval | alert_detail -> recovery_override } }, with `protection` itself reaching `identity_detail` and `alert_detail`. Each re-homed screen's `onback` returns to the door it now hangs off, which is the only spatial model this flat step union has. Two surfaces are reachable from more than one place, so each records where it came from rather than assuming: `alert_detail` (home's card strip, the identity panel's critical status, or a Protection row) via `alertReturnStep`, and `identity_detail` (the home list or a Protection row) via `identityReturnStep`. A fixed back path would eject the user out of the identity they were standing in, or out of the list they were working through. On mount, checks for existing identities via `listIdentities()` and skips to `home` if any exist. Registers a `visibilitychange` listener that calls `checkIdentityStatus()` when the app returns to foreground while on the `home` **or** `protection` step — Protection's whole subject is how fresh the reading is, so it is the worst place to sit showing a stale one. **Alarm takeover landing:** that check — on launch and on every foreground — hands its answer to `$lib/alarm-landing`'s `decideAlarmLanding`, and the page lands on the alarm rather than leaving it behind the protection strip: one alarmed identity opens `alert_detail`, more than one opens `protection` (already ordered most-urgent-first by `$lib/protection`). Landing precedence is the `onMount` ordering itself — a stranded removal and a pending recovery epilogue are resolved first and the takeover runs only in the branch where neither did, because interrupted key-material handling outranks re-showing an alarm the user has already been told about; `landOnAlarm` re-checks that the app is still on `home`/`protection` before it moves, since the directory round trip can land after the user has navigated. Every takeover is dismissible: both landings' exits read **"Not now"** (`AlertDetailScreen`'s `backLabel`, `ProtectionScreen`'s `takeover`, both driven by the `alarmTakeover` flag `goTo` clears) and returns to a home the strip and card treatments already render in alarm state. Alarms the takeover has presented are recorded in the in-session `shownAlarms` set keyed by `alarmKey` (DID + sorted change CIDs), so a dismissed alarm does not re-take the app on the next foreground but a *new* unauthorized operation against the same identity does. The set is deliberately not persisted — an attack must not be dismissible once, forever

**Guarantees:**
- SSR is disabled globally (`ssr = false` in `src/routes/+layout.ts`); the frontend is a fully static SPA loaded from disk by WKWebView
- Build output lands in `dist/` (configured via `pages: 'dist'` in `svelte.config.js`)
- Frontend calls Tauri commands only through the `src/lib/ipc/` modules (imported from `$lib/ipc`) — no raw `invoke()` calls in page components
- PDS error codes from `create_account` are mapped back to the originating screen (e.g. EXPIRED_CODE -> claim_code step, EMAIL_TAKEN -> email step)

**Expects:**
- `pnpm install` has been run in `apps/identity-wallet/`
- Node.js 22.x is in PATH (provided by the Nix dev shell)

### Rust Backend (src-tauri/)

**Exposes:**
- `src/lib.rs::create_account(claim_code, email, handle) -> Result<CreateAccountResult, CreateAccountError>` — Tauri IPC command: gets or creates device key via `device_key::get_or_create()`, POSTs to PDS `/v1/accounts/mobile`, stores tokens in Keychain on success
- `src/lib.rs::perform_did_ceremony(handle: String, password: String) -> Result<DIDCeremonyResult, DIDCeremonyError>` — Tauri IPC command running the **client-share ceremony** (ceremony inversion): fetches the PDS signing key (GET /v1/repo-signing-key), loads-or-generates the client-side share set via `share_ceremony::load_or_create` (recovery seed + `derive_recovery_keypair` + 2-of-3 v2 envelope split, staged in the `ceremony-staging` Keychain slot BEFORE any network call so a retry reuses the identical set/set_id), builds the signed did:plc genesis op via `crypto::build_did_plc_genesis_op_multi_rotation_with_external_signer` with `rotationKeys = [device, recovery, PDS]` (ADR-0027) using the device key as signer, POSTs the op + password + `recoveryKey` + `escrowShare` (the Share 2 envelope — the only share Custos ever sees) to POST /v1/dids, persists DID + upgraded session token in Keychain, writes the wallet-generated Share 1 envelope to the per-DID slot `recovery-share-1:{did}` with a read-back verify (same convention as the re-key flow, so a second identity's ceremony cannot overwrite the first's Share 1), and returns `{ did, share3, share3Words }` to the frontend
- `src/lib.rs::confirm_share_backup(did: String) -> Result<(), ShareBackupError>` — Tauri IPC command: the ceremony teardown gate. Verifies the ceremony DID's Share 1 is durably present in `recovery-share-1:{did}` (else `SHARE_NOT_STORED` — the staging slot must not be destroyed while it is the seed's only home), then deletes the `ceremony-staging` slot (the seed's and Share 2's last local copy). The `did` is threaded from the ceremony result so the check reads the exact identity just created (mirrors the re-key epilogue's `confirm_rekey`). Idempotent; invoked by the frontend when the Shamir backup screen's confirmation completes
- `src/share_ceremony.rs` — client-side share generation module: `CeremonyShareSet` (recovery key did:key + the three base32 envelope strings + the Share 3 word phrase, all share material in `Zeroizing`), `load_or_create(handle, pds_url)` (reuse a valid staged set or generate + stage a fresh one; the staging record stores the three envelopes only — the seed is recomputed via `combine_envelopes(share1, share2)` on load), `clear_staging()` (idempotent teardown), `STAGING_ACCOUNT` (`"ceremony-staging"`). **Fail-closed staging contract:** only a genuinely absent slot, or one staged for different ceremony inputs (a new handle/PDS is the user's explicit abandonment of the old attempt), permits fresh generation; a present-but-unreadable/corrupt record errors with `StagingCorrupt` and preserves the slot — it may be the exact set a prior attempt already bound to a genesis op and escrowed, so overwriting it would permanently destroy the recovery seed
- `src/share_recovery.rs` — the "Recover existing identity" ceremony (10 Tauri IPC commands), the consuming inverse of `share_ceremony.rs`: `start_share_recovery(identifier)` (resolve handle/did:plc via plc.directory, then auto-load Share 1 via `auto_load_share1`: the resolved DID's iCloud-synchronizable per-DID slot, then its device-local per-DID slot, then the legacy global `recovery-share-1`, taking the first tier holding a valid v2 index-1 envelope), `add_recovery_share(share)` (base32 or word-phrase entry; SHARE_CHECKSUM, SHARE_SET_MISMATCH — with both set_ids — and DUPLICATE_SHARE are distinct, pre-combine errors), `remove_recovery_share(index)`, the escrow-assisted path client `initiate_escrow_release()` / `request_escrow_release(otp?)` (targets the account's own PDS endpoint from the authoritative DID state; OTP opens the release, OTP-less calls poll the pending window; the server's uniform 401 maps to RELEASE_UNAUTHORIZED), `verify_recovery_shares()` (combine → `derive_recovery_keypair` → compare against the **authoritative plc.directory audit log**, never a cached doc — mismatch is SHARES_DO_NOT_MATCH_IDENTITY, before anything signs), `recover_identity()` (fresh per-DID device key; the recovery key signs the rotation op installing it at `rotationKeys[0]`; talks ONLY to plc.directory — the fully-sovereign path makes zero PDS requests until re-escrow; idempotent on retry; durably stages the epilogue before returning), `run_recovery_epilogue(skip_escrow?)` (resumable: swap the new recovery key into `rotationKeys[1]` signed by the new device key → re-escrow the new Share 2 over a stored-or-fresh device-key sovereign session → rewrite the recovered DID's per-DID slot `recovery-share-1:{did}` with read-back verify; each step recorded in the durable `recovery-epilogue` Keychain record as it completes), `get_pending_recovery_epilogue()` (launch-time resume hook), `confirm_recovery_backup()` (teardown gate mirroring `confirm_share_backup`; destroys the epilogue record only after the NEW Share 1 is verified durable in the per-DID slot). Session state (`AppState.share_recovery_state`) is in-memory by design — the pre-anchor phase restarts from the entry screen; only the epilogue persists. `ShareRecoveryError` serializes as `{ code: "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE" }` with camelCase fields
- `src/lib.rs::{prepare_did_web_ceremony,complete_did_web_ceremony}` — did:web sibling ceremony: obtains the same device key and pending account's reserved repo key, lets the frontend compose/export the reviewed `did.json`, then submits it to `POST /v1/dids` only after it is externally resolvable. A revoked refresh (400/401) and a host change both delete the dead record; a rate limit keeps it. Coalescing is a re-read (not a shared future): the second caller for one DID waits on the lock, then re-loads the freshly-persisted record — so a refresh token can never be raced into replay detection. Does NOT reuse `OAuthClient::refresh_token_bearer` (which is in-memory-only by design) — the provider owns refresh+persist. Three further rules keep the log honest: a **failed** check leaves an identity's previous `last_verified_at` standing (the last verification is still a fact); only identities present in the sweep survive the fold (a removed DID leaves the log on the next pass, and the record can never resurrect one); and identical *foreground* passes within five minutes coalesce, so ordinary navigation — which fires a check on launch, on foreground, and on entering the identity screen — cannot evict the background sweeps the log exists to evidence. A successful fetch **replaces that host's set wholesale** — that single choice is what implements add-new / retire / revoke: a revoked key vanishes from the device at its next contact, which is the entire short-compromise-window property. A 501 (host runs no relay) and a 503 (instance cannot read its own keys) both leave the stored set untouched: neither is a revocation, and clearing on a misconfigured deploy would strip every device that checked in during it. Two ordinary "no" answers are **outcomes, not errors** — `AWAITING_APNS_TOKEN` (simulator, denied permission, or the token simply not delivered yet) and `UNSUPPORTED` (a 501) — so onboarding has nothing to catch. `NotificationsError` (SESSION_LOCKED, RATE_LIMITED, IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND, KEY_GENERATION_FAILED, KEYCHAIN_ERROR, SERVER_ERROR, NETWORK_ERROR) serialized as `{ code: "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE" }` with camelCase fields

The IMP is a bare C function pointer with no capture, so the callback reads the `AppHandle` from a `OnceLock` written during `setup` (the unit-of-global shape `IdentityStore` uses). On a **changed** token it re-registers every managed identity; an unchanged one (iOS re-delivers on every launch) does nothing, since a round trip per identity per launch would only rewrite rows that already say this. Every part with logic worth testing lives in `notifications.rs` — this file is compiled only by the `aarch64-apple-ios` cross-compile and exercised only on a device
