<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <!--
    The Notification Service Extension's iOS code-signing entitlements.

    Referenced by the shared XcodeGen template (scripts/ios/project.yml) as the NSE target's
    CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS build setting, path-relative to gen/apple. Unlike the app's
    Entitlements.ios.plist this does NOT go through ios-postinit's Patch H: that patch exists
    because tauri-cli's build-time codesign reads the app target's default entitlements path
    regardless of the template. Tauri signs only the app; the extension is signed by Xcode
    from this setting, so the tracked file is used directly and there is nothing to install.

    ONE entitlement, and it is the whole reason the extension can do anything: the shared
    keychain access group that MM-419 put the notification private key and the pinned
    sender-key set into. Without it the extension's Keychain queries search only its own
    implicit group (the extension's own bundle id), find nothing, and every push renders as
    the unverified notice.

    ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING, exactly as in the app's entitlements: iOS searches EVERY entitled
    group on an unqualified read and files an unqualified write into the FIRST. Neither
    process names a group in its queries (that would mean discovering the team's
    AppIdentifierPrefix at runtime, adding a failure mode to the one path that must work on a
    locked screen), so `org.obsign.shared` must be first here and in the app, or the
    breadcrumbs the extension writes land somewhere the app cannot read them. The legacy
    group is listed for the same indefinite-readability reason given there — see ADR-0030 and
    keychain.rs's `entitlement_declares_stable_group_first`.

    Deliberately ABSENT: `aps-environment`. That is an app entitlement, not an extension one —
    the app obtains the device token, the extension only decrypts what arrives. And no iCloud
    container: the extension touches no backup.

    PORTAL WORK: an app extension is a separate bundle
    (dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService), so it needs its own explicit App ID
    and its own distribution profile before the TestFlight lane can sign a build that embeds
    it. `keychain-access-groups` itself needs no registration — a provisioning profile
    authorizes the whole team prefix via a <TeamID>.* wildcard. See docs/ios-cicd.md.
  -->
  <key>keychain-access-groups</key>
  <array>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared</string>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>
</dict>
</plist>

  # console declares no keychain-access-groups and registers no notification keys, so
  # its extension would read an empty shared group and render the unverified notice for

  #

  # cargo-mobile2 helper, so it survives a tauri-cli bump that changes the helper set.
  # The literal is the same bundle id `just bundle-identity-check` pins; a rename has to
  # move both, which is why that script's rename checklist names this file.
  {{#if (eq app.identifier "dev.malpercio.identitywallet")}}
  {{app.name}}_NSE:
    type: app-extension
    platform: iOS
    sources:
      # ONE shared implementation at the repo root — no per-app copy to drift, the same
      # arrangement as scripts/ios/. Swift-only: decryption is CryptoKit, so there is no
      # second Rust staticlib and none of the toolchain machinery the app target needs.
      - path: ../../../../../ios/NotificationService
    info:
      path: {{app.name}}_NSE/Info.plist
      properties:
        CFBundleDisplayName: {{app.stylized-name}} Notifications
        CFBundleShortVersionString: {{apple.bundle-version-short}}
        CFBundleVersion: "{{apple.bundle-version}}"
        NSExtension:
          NSExtensionPointIdentifier: com.apple.usernotifications.service
          NSExtensionPrincipalClass: $(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).NotificationService
    settings:
      base:
        PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER: {{app.identifier}}.NotificationService
        # Pinned rather than derived from the target name: it is half of
        # NSExtensionPrincipalClass above, and the name the test bundle's sources
        # compile under. A rename that silently changed it would leave iOS unable to
        # instantiate the principal class — a failure that looks exactly like a push
        # that never arrived.
        PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME: NotificationService
        PRODUCT_NAME: {{app.name}}_NSE
        # Path-relative to gen/apple, i.e. apps/<app>/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist.
        # Referenced directly rather than installed by ios-postinit's Patch H: that patch
        # exists because tauri's build-time codesign reads the APP target's default
        # entitlements path whatever the template says. Tauri signs only the app — Xcode
        # signs the extension from this setting — so the tracked file is used as-is.
        CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS: ../../Entitlements.NSE.plist

        DEVELOPMENT_TEAM: {{apple.development-team}}
        {{/if}}

        # extension is archived by the same build, so it meets the same sandbox and
        # entitlements-restamp behavior.
        ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING: "NO"
        CODE_SIGN_ALLOW_ENTITLEMENTS_MODIFICATION: "YES"
    dependencies:
      # The only framework worth naming: Swift autolinks CryptoKit, Security and
      # Foundation from their `import`s, and this one matches what Apple's own NSE
      # template declares.
      - sdk: UserNotifications.framework

  {{app.name}}_NSETests:
    type: bundle.unit-test
    platform: iOS

      # from the extension target. An app-extension target has no testable module to
      # import (there is no TEST_HOST an extension can be loaded into), so recompiling
      # ~400 lines is what makes these logic tests runnable at all — and it keeps them
      # host-independent, so `⌘U` needs no push, no device, and no registered key.
      - path: ../../../../../ios/NotificationService
      - path: ../../../../../ios/NotificationServiceTests
      # The Rust-generated golden HPKE vectors, referenced IN PLACE — there is no copy
      # under ios/ that could fall out of step with the crate that produces them.
      - path: ../../../../../crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json
        buildPhase: resources
    settings:
      base:
        PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER: {{app.identifier}}.NotificationServiceTests
        {{#if apple.development-team}}
        DEVELOPMENT_TEAM: {{apple.development-team}}
        {{/if}}
        ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING: "NO"
  {{/if}}

I need to add the test target to the app scheme so that running tests with ⌘U works properly. The app target already has a scheme configuration with environment variables, so I can add `testTargets` there to wire up the test target to the app's scheme.

Actually, a cleaner approach is to create a dedicated top-level scheme just for the NSE tests. This way I can build and run only the test bundle without triggering the slow Rust build. I'll add a gated `schemes:` block at the end of the file that defines a test-only scheme with the NSE test target.

I also need to remove the `@testable import NotificationService` from the test files since the sources are already compiled in.

input.command:
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && cat >> scripts/ios/project.yml <<'YAML'

# A dedicated scheme for the extension's logic tests, so `⌘U` (or `xcodebuild test
# -scheme <app>_NSETests`) runs them WITHOUT building the app — which would mean the
# whole Rust staticlib, the frontend bundle, and the JSON-RPC dance with a running
# `cargo tauri ios dev`. Attaching them to the app's scheme instead would have made the
# fixture cross-check cost a full app build every time.
{{#if (eq app.identifier "dev.malpercio.identitywallet")}}
schemes:
  {{app.name}}_NSETests:
    build:
      targets:
        {{app.name}}_NSETests: [test]
    test:
      targets:
        - {{app.name}}_NSETests
{{/if}}
YAML

1	# ezpds-ios-template — shared custom XcodeGen project template for BOTH iOS apps
2	# (identity-wallet, admin-companion), wired via `bundle > iOS > template` in each
3	# app's tauri.conf.json. `cargo tauri ios init` renders this Handlebars template
4	# into gen/apple/project.yml on EVERY init (unconditionally, unlike the other
5	# generated files, which are only created when missing), then runs
6	# `xcodegen generate` to rebuild project.pbxproj from it. That makes this file —
7	# not the gitignored generated project — the durable home of the Xcode-project
8	# workarounds that ios-postinit.sh used to re-apply by regex-patching the pbxproj
9	# (see docs/ios-upstream-bugs.md for each workaround's upstream bug).
10	#
11	# upstream-version: tauri-cli 2.11.4
12	# Forked from crates/tauri-cli/templates/mobile/ios/project.yml at that tag; the
13	# pristine copy is committed next to this file as upstream-project.yml so the fork
14	# can be diffed against it. When bumping the tauri-cli pin (the `cargo binstall
15	# tauri-cli --version` lines in .github/workflows/*.yml), refresh
16	# upstream-project.yml from the new tag, re-merge upstream's changes into this
17	# fork, and bump the upstream-version line above — scripts/ios-template-check.sh
18	# (part of `just ci` / `ci-pds`) fails until the versions are back in lockstep.
19	#
20	# ezpds changes vs upstream (each marked with an `ezpds:` comment inline):
21	#   1. Externals gets `buildPhase: none` — keeps libapp.a out of Copy Bundle
22	#      Resources (App Store rejects a raw staticlib in the .app; tauri#13578).
23	#   2. Target settings force ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING off (macOS 26 blocks
24	#      Cargo's readdir under the Run Script sandbox), allow the spurious
25	#      "entitlements modified during build" (per-build pbxproj restamp race), and
26	#      link the Apple frameworks the Rust staticlib needs via OTHER_LDFLAGS

1	// The cross-implementation check the golden fixtures were generated for.
2	//
3	// `crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` is sealed by the Rust `hpke`
4	// crate and opened, here, by CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix has no test vector for this exact
5	// suite (A.3 is AES-128; CryptoKit's only P-256 suite forces AES-256), so nothing else proves
6	// the two implementations agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and
7	// the key encodings. The Rust side asserts these same vectors round-trip in
8	// `notify_hpke_vectors.rs`; between them, a drift on either side fails a test instead of
9	// producing devices that silently stop decrypting.
10	//
11	// The fixture file is referenced IN PLACE by the XcodeGen template — there is no copy in this
12	// directory to fall out of date with the crate.
13	//
14	// Not run by CI: `ios-pr-check` stops short of xcodebuild (no simulator, no archive), so this
15	// is a `⌘U` in Xcode or `xcodebuild test`. That is the same footing as the on-device demo the
16	// issue's acceptance names, and the reason the pure logic below is also covered by tests that
17	// need no crypto at all.

# --- The Notification Service Extension (ezpds change 5) ---
# The extension is what makes an end-to-end-encrypted push readable: it HPKE-opens the sealed
# payload with the key MM-419 put in the shared keychain group. Every piece below is load-
# bearing in a way that fails SILENTLY if dropped — a re-rendered template missing the target
# leaves the app installing happily and showing "couldn't verify" for every notification
# forever, with nothing in any log to say the extension was never built.
require 'type: app-extension' "the NSE target (a sealed push renders as the unverified notice without it)"
require 'NSExtensionPointIdentifier: com.apple.usernotifications.service' "the NSE's extension point (iOS would not route pushes to it)"
require 'PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME: NotificationService' "half of NSExtensionPrincipalClass — a drift here means iOS cannot instantiate the extension"
require '- path: ../../../../../ios/NotificationService' "the shared Swift sources, referenced in place"
require 'CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS: ../../Entitlements.NSE.plist' "the NSE's shared-keychain entitlement (without it every Keychain read finds nothing)"
# The embed dependency, not the target definition, is what puts the extension in the archive.
if ! grep -qF -- '- target: {{app.name}}_NSE' "${TEMPLATE}"; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the app target no longer embeds {{app.name}}_NSE; the extension would be built but never shipped" >&2
  fail=1
fi
# The gate is what keeps admin-companion from needing a second App ID + profile + secret for
# an extension it cannot use (see the template's comment and MM-421). If it is ever removed,
# it must be removed deliberately, alongside the console's shared keychain group.
if ! grep -qF -- '{{#if (eq app.identifier "dev.malpercio.identitywallet")}}' "${TEMPLATE}"; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the NSE is no longer gated to the wallet's bundle id; admin-companion would need its own extension App ID and provisioning profile before either TestFlight lane could sign a build" >&2
  fail=1
fi
# The interop test's fixture is referenced in place, so there is no copy to drift from the
# crate that generates it.
require '- path: ../../../../../crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json' "the Rust golden HPKE vectors the CryptoKit cross-check opens"
for source in ios/NotificationService/NotificationService.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyCrypto.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyEnvelope.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyKeychain.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift \
              ios/NotificationServiceTests/NotifyFixtureTests.swift; do
  if [ ! -f "${REPO_ROOT}/${source}" ]; then
    echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — ${source} missing (the template compiles the whole ios/NotificationService tree)" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
# The extension's entitlements are its ONLY reach into the app's Keychain, and the ORDER is
# the mechanism: neither process names an access group in its queries, so iOS files an
# unqualified write into the FIRST entitled group. If org.obsign.shared is not first in BOTH
# files, the breadcrumbs the extension writes land where the app cannot read them.
NSE_ENT="${REPO_ROOT}/apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist"
if [ ! -f "${NSE_ENT}" ]; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — ${NSE_ENT} missing (the NSE target's CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS points at it)" >&2
  fail=1
elif ! command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ios-template-check: WARN — python3 unavailable; skipping the NSE keychain-group order check" >&2
elif ! python3 - "${NSE_ENT}" <<'PY'
import plistlib, sys
with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as handle:
    groups = plistlib.load(handle).get("keychain-access-groups", [])
sys.exit(0 if groups and groups[0] == "$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared" else 1)
PY
then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the NSE entitlements must list \$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared FIRST; an unqualified write otherwise lands in a group the app cannot read (ADR-0030)" >&2
  fail=1
fi
# The extension only ever needs the shared keychain group. aps-environment is an APP
# entitlement (the app obtains the token; the extension only decrypts), and a stray iCloud
# grant here would widen the reach of the one process that runs on a locked screen.
if grep -qiE 'aps-environment|icloud|ubiquity' "${NSE_ENT}" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the NSE entitlements declare more than the shared keychain group (least privilege: it obtains no push token and touches no backup)" >&2
  fail=1
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ios-template-check.sh — keep the forked XcodeGen template in lockstep with the
# pinned tauri-cli. Linux-runnable; part of `just ci` / `just ci-pds`.
#
# scripts/ios/project.yml is a fork of tauri-cli's built-in iOS project template
# (rendered into gen/apple/project.yml on every `cargo tauri ios init` via
# `bundle > iOS > template`). Replacing upstream's template wholesale means upstream
# changes to it — new build settings, search-path fixes — no longer reach us
# automatically. This gate closes that hole at the only moment drift can enter:
# when someone bumps the tauri-cli pin in the workflows without re-merging the
# upstream template, the versions disagree and CI fails with instructions.
#
# It also asserts the structural invariants the macOS-side ios-check verifies in
# the *generated* project — here checked in the *source* template, so a Linux PR
# that breaks the template fails before it ever reaches the macOS lanes.
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
REPO_ROOT="$(cd "${SCRIPT_DIR}/.." && pwd)"
TEMPLATE="${REPO_ROOT}/scripts/ios/project.yml"
PRISTINE="${REPO_ROOT}/scripts/ios/upstream-project.yml"

fail=0

if [ ! -f "${TEMPLATE}" ]; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — ${TEMPLATE} missing" >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [ ! -f "${PRISTINE}" ]; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — ${PRISTINE} missing (the pristine upstream copy used to diff the fork)" >&2
  fail=1
fi

# --- Version lockstep: template stamp == every workflow's tauri-cli pin ---
stamped="$(sed -n 's/^# upstream-version: tauri-cli \([0-9][0-9.]*\)$/\1/p' "${TEMPLATE}")"
if [ -z "${stamped}" ]; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — no '# upstream-version: tauri-cli X.Y.Z' line in ${TEMPLATE}" >&2
  fail=1
else
  pins_found=0
  # The tauri-cli pin now lives in the shared runner-preamble composite action
  # (.github/actions/ios-setup/action.yml) — one home for all iOS lanes. Scan it
  # alongside the workflow files so a pin lingering in either location is still caught.
  for wf in "${REPO_ROOT}"/.github/workflows/*.yml "${REPO_ROOT}"/.github/actions/ios-setup/action.yml; do
    [ -f "${wf}" ] || continue
    pin="$(sed -n "s/.*cargo binstall -y --locked tauri-cli --version '\([0-9][0-9.]*\)'.*/\1/p" "${wf}")"
    [ -z "${pin}" ] && continue
    pins_found=$((pins_found + 1))
    if [ "${pin}" != "${stamped}" ]; then
      echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — $(basename "${wf}") pins tauri-cli ${pin}, but scripts/ios/project.yml is forked from ${stamped}." >&2
      echo "  To bump: fetch the new tag's crates/tauri-cli/templates/mobile/ios/project.yml into" >&2
      echo "  scripts/ios/upstream-project.yml, re-merge upstream's changes into scripts/ios/project.yml" >&2
      echo "  (the ezpds changes are marked with 'ezpds:' comments), and update its upstream-version line." >&2
      fail=1
    fi
  done

import re, sys, yaml

SRC = open("scripts/ios/project.yml").read()

CTX_WALLET = {
    "app.name": "Obsign", "app.identifier": "dev.malpercio.identitywallet",
    "app.stylized-name": "Obsign", "app.asset-dir": "assets",
    "apple.ios-version": "17.0", "apple.development-team": "ABCDE12345",
    "apple.bundle-version-short": "0.9.2", "apple.bundle-version": "2",
    "lib-output-file-name": "libapp.a", "tauri-binary": "cargo-tauri",
    "tauri-binary-args-str": "tauri ios xcode-script",
}
CTX_ADMIN = dict(CTX_WALLET, **{
    "app.name": "AdminCompanion", "app.identifier": "dev.malpercio.admincompanion",
    "app.stylized-name": "Admin Companion",
})
LISTS = {
    "ios-frameworks": ["SystemConfiguration", "UserNotifications"],
    "ios-valid-archs": ["arm64"], "file-groups": ["Sources"],
    "asset-catalogs": [], "ios-additional-targets": [], "ios-libraries": [],
    "ios-vendor-frameworks": [], "ios-vendor-sdks": [], "apple.plist-pairs": [],
    "ios-command-line-arguments": [], "ios-pre-build-scripts": [],
    "ios-post-compile-scripts": [], "ios-post-build-scripts": [],
}

def render(ctx):
    text = SRC
    # helpers used as inline expressions
    text = text.replace("{{join file-groups}}", "Sources")
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{~?#each ios-valid-archs\}\}(.*?)\{\{/each\}\}",
                  lambda m: m.group(1).replace("{{this}}", "arm64"), text, flags=re.S)
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{~?#each ios-frameworks\}\}(.*?)\{\{/each\}\}",
                  lambda m: "".join(m.group(1).replace("{{this}}", f) for f in LISTS["ios-frameworks"]),
                  text, flags=re.S)
    # empty #each / falsy #if blocks vanish
    for name in LISTS:
        text = re.sub(r"\{\{~?#each " + re.escape(name) + r"\}\}.*?\{\{~?/each~?\}\}", "", text, flags=re.S)
        text = re.sub(r"\{\{~?#if " + re.escape(name) + r"\}\}.*?\{\{~?/if~?\}\}", "", text, flags=re.S)
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{~?#if this\.[a-z-]+\}\}.*?\{\{/if\}\}", "", text, flags=re.S)
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{~?#if ios-[a-z-]+\}\}.*?\{\{~?/if~?\}\}", "", text, flags=re.S)
    # the bundle-id gate
    def gate(m):
        body = m.group(2)
        return body if ctx["app.identifier"] == m.group(1) else ""
    text = re.sub(r'\{\{~?#if \(eq app\.identifier "([^"]+)"\)\}\}(.*?)\{\{~?/if\}\}', gate, text, flags=re.S)
    # development-team (truthy)
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{#if apple\.development-team\}\}(.*?)\{\{/if\}\}", lambda m: m.group(1), text, flags=re.S)
    for key, value in ctx.items():
        text = text.replace("{{" + key + "}}", value).replace("{{ " + key + " }}", value)
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{[^}]*\}\}", "", text)
    return text

for name, ctx in (("wallet", CTX_WALLET), ("admin", CTX_ADMIN)):
    out = render(ctx)
    open(f"{sys.argv[1]}/{name}.yml", "w").write(out)
    doc = yaml.safe_load(out)
    targets = sorted(doc.get("targets", {}))
    schemes = sorted((doc.get("schemes") or {}))
    print(f"{name}: YAML OK  targets={targets}  schemes={schemes}")
    app = doc["targets"][f"{ctx['app.name']}_iOS"]
    embeds = [d for d in app.get("dependencies", []) if isinstance(d, dict) and "target" in d]
    print(f"   app embeds: {embeds}")

I'm realizing the issue is with my test renderer's regex pattern — it's using non-greedy matching that stops at the first closing `{{/if}}` it encounters, but when there are nested conditionals inside the block, it prematurely terminates at the inner closing tag instead of the outer one. Handlebars itself probably handles this correctly, so this is a problem with how I'm parsing the template in my test setup.

The fix is to reorder my substitutions: resolve the development-team conditional first before processing the gate, which should prevent the nesting issue from affecting my validation. Let me restructure and test again.

input.new_string:
# The Notification Service Extension. Rendered by the template only for the app whose bundle
# id matches the gate there (the wallet today — see that file, and MM-421 for the console), so
# this reads the same source of truth rather than restating which app is which.
#
# Everything here fails SILENTLY if the template did not apply: the app installs, launches, and
# behaves normally, and every sealed notification renders "couldn't verify" forever with nothing
# anywhere saying the extension was never built. That is why the pbxproj is checked and not just
# the project.yml — a rendered-but-not-generated project would pass the template check upstream.
NSE_ENT="${APP_DIR}/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist"
if [ -f "${NSE_ENT}" ]; then
  if ! grep -q 'com.apple.product-type.app-extension' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "ios-check: FAIL — no app-extension target in the project; sealed notifications would all render as unverified ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
  # The embed is a separate fact from the target existing: without the Embed Foundation
  # Extensions copy phase the extension is built and then left out of the .app.
  if ! grep -qE '_NSE\.appex in (Embed|Copy)' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "ios-check: FAIL — the NSE .appex is not embedded into the app bundle ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
  if ! grep -qF 'CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS = "../../Entitlements.NSE.plist"' "${PBXPROJ}" \
     && ! grep -qF 'CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS = ../../Entitlements.NSE.plist' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "ios-check: FAIL — the NSE target does not point at ${NSE_ENT}; its Keychain reads would find nothing ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
  # Half of NSExtensionPrincipalClass. A drift makes iOS unable to instantiate the extension,
  # which looks exactly like a push that never arrived.
  if ! grep -q 'PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME = NotificationService' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "ios-check: FAIL — the NSE's PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME is not NotificationService ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
  NSE_PLIST="$(dirname "${PBXPROJ}")/../$(basename "$(dirname "$(dirname "${PBXPROJ}")")" .xcodeproj)_NSE/Info.plist"
  NSE_PLIST="$(dirname "${PBXPROJ}")/../"*_NSE/Info.plist
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086 # deliberate glob: the target dir is named from {{app.name}}
  for plist in ${NSE_PLIST}; do
    [ -f "${plist}" ] || continue
    if command -v plutil >/dev/null 2>&1 && ! plutil -lint "${plist}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      echo "ios-check: FAIL — ${plist} is not a valid plist ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
      fail=1
    fi
  done
fi

# Non-crate entries every iOS lane must carry regardless of the crate graph.
# (Each lane additionally watches its own workflow file(s), added in expected_for
# via watched_workflows_for.)
#   Cargo.toml / Cargo.lock     — a shared-dependency bump can change what the apps build
#   justfile                    — the root justfile; the lanes' build steps are just recipes
#   just/release.just, just/ios.just — the imported recipe files the root justfile pulls
#                                 in (the iOS build recipes now live in just/ios.just); a
#                                 broken import fails `just` at parse time for every lane
#   scripts/ios/**              — the shared iOS toolchain/patch scripts
#   .github/actions/ios-setup/**— the shared runner-preamble composite action all three
#                                 lanes use (toolchain, cache, tauri-cli pin, brew shim)
#   rust-toolchain.toml         — pins the toolchain + iOS targets
INFRA=(
  "Cargo.toml"
  "Cargo.lock"
  "justfile"
  "just/release.just"
  "just/ios.just"
  "scripts/ios/**"
  ".github/actions/ios-setup/**"
  "rust-toolchain.toml"
)

# Workflow file(s) whose changes must re-trigger a given lane. Normally a lane just

  printf '.github/workflows/%s\n' "$1"
  case "$1" in
    ios-testflight.yml | admin-testflight.yml)

  esac
}

content.text:
`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Why the breadcrumb log's version tag reuses `PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION`:** both documents are written by whoever is running and read by whoever is running — but the pin store has one author (the app) while the failure log has *two independently-versioned bundles* touching it. That's why `reason` stayed a `String` on the Rust side while the TypeScript union uses `(string & {})`: a strict enum would silently drop the one entry the user is asking about.

**The `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME: NotificationService` pin isn't cosmetic.** It's literally half of `NSExtensionPrincipalClass: $(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).NotificationService`. If XcodeGen derived it from the target name (`Obsign_NSE`), iOS would fail to instantiate the class — and that failure is indistinguishable from a push that never arrived, which is why `ios-check` greps the pbxproj for it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

---
# Changelog fragments

Every pull request that changes a shipped surface must add a short Markdown fragment:

```text
changelog.d/<id>.<type>.md
```

- `<id>` is the Linear issue identifier in lowercase (for example, `mm-358`). If a
  change has no Linear issue, use the pull request number (for example, `271`).
--- gate:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Require a changelog fragment *added by the change itself* when a PR changes a shipped
# surface (fragments already sitting in changelog.d/ from other work don't satisfy it).
# CHANGELOG_BASE_REF is set to the PR base SHA in CI; an explicit first argument is
# convenient for local checks. With neither, fragment validity is still checked but
# presence is not required because there is no trustworthy comparison range.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

base_ref="${1:-${CHANGELOG_BASE_REF:-}}"
fragment_dir="changelog.d"
fragment_re='^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*\.(added|changed|fixed|removed|security)\.md$'

fail=0
fragment_count=0
while IFS= read -r fragment; do
  name="${fragment##*/}"
  if ! [[ "$name" =~ $fragment_re ]]; then
    echo "✗ invalid changelog fragment '$fragment' — expected <id>.<added|changed|fixed|removed|security>.md" >&2
    fail=1
    continue
  fi
  if ! grep -q '[^[:space:]]' "$fragment"; then
    echo "✗ changelog fragment '$fragment' is empty" >&2
    fail=1
    continue
  fi
  fragment_count=$((fragment_count + 1))
done < <(find "$fragment_dir" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.md' ! -name README.md | sort)

if [ "$fail" -ne 0 ]; then
  exit 1
fi

if [ -z "$base_ref" ]; then
  echo "✓ $fragment_count valid changelog fragment(s); no base ref supplied, so presence was not evaluated"
  exit 0
fi

content.content: Obsign can now receive the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. On first launch it asks permission, generates a notification key that never leaves the device, and tells each of your identities' servers where to reach it — so a notification can be sealed to your phone specifically, and read nowhere else. What that protects is the notification's *content*: neither the relay in the middle nor Apple can see what one says. It does not hide that a notification happened — your own server is told which device to reach, and Apple necessarily handles delivery — so what is kept from everyone in between is the message, not the fact of it. The key is used for nothing else: it never signs anything, and losing it costs you banners rather than an identity. Obsign also re-checks which signing keys your instance publishes every time it contacts it. That is what keeps the window short if one of those keys is ever compromised — a key your operator revokes stops being trusted by your phone the next time the two talk, without you doing anything. Registration is quiet by design: on a simulator, or for an identity hosted somewhere that runs no relay, Obsign simply carries on with notifications switched off rather than reporting an error you cannot act on. Both Obsign and Admin Companion now require iOS 17, which is where Apple's encrypted-notification support begins.

input.content:
Obsign now reads the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. Until now your phone could receive one but not open it, so every notification arrived as a placeholder; a small extension bundled with the app now unseals each one the moment it arrives — on the lock screen, without waking the app, and without the relay in the middle or Apple ever seeing the text. What you read is what your server wrote.

When a notification *cannot* be opened, Obsign says so plainly rather than showing you something that looks genuine. iOS does not let an app silently discard a notification, so anything that fails to unseal — a relay sending noise, a message signed with a key your phone has not seen, or one arriving before you have unlocked your phone since restarting it — appears as an explicit "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance". It is never dressed up as real content, which is what stops whoever carries your notifications from being able to put words in your server's mouth.

Because that notice on its own cannot tell you *which* of those happened, Settings gains a Notifications section that can. It counts the recent failures and names the likely cause in plain language — and, where there is something to do, says what: a key mismatch is usually fixed by opening one of your identities, since Obsign refreshes the keys on every contact with your server, while a run of unrecognisable notifications points at the relay rather than at anything of yours being at risk. Once you have dealt with it, you can clear the record so the next real report is not lost in an old one.

Obsign now reads the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. Until now your phone could receive one but not open it, so every notification arrived as a placeholder; a small extension bundled with the app now unseals each one the moment it arrives — on the lock screen, without waking the app, and without the relay in the middle or Apple ever seeing the text. What you read is what your server wrote.

When a notification *cannot* be opened, Obsign says so plainly rather than showing you something that looks genuine. iOS does not let an app silently discard a notification, so anything that fails to unseal — a relay sending noise, a message signed with a key your phone has not seen, or one arriving before you have unlocked your phone since restarting it — appears as an explicit "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance". It is never dressed up as real content, which is what stops whoever carries your notifications from being able to put words in your server's mouth.

Because that notice on its own cannot tell you *which* of those happened, Settings gains a Notifications section that can. It counts the recent failures and names the likely cause in plain language — and, where there is something to do, says what: a key mismatch is usually fixed by opening one of your identities, since Obsign refreshes the keys on every contact with your server, while a run of unrecognisable notifications points at the relay rather than at anything of yours being at risk. Once you have dealt with it, you can clear the record so the next real report is not lost in an old one.

# Shared iOS Swift sources

Last verified: 2026-07-27

## Purpose

Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
notifications on arrival.

It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
inputs are shared too. MM-421 gives the operator console an extension from these same sources.

## Contracts

### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)

**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.

**Guarantees:**
- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.

**Expects:**
- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs` (MM-419).
- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `NotificationService.swift` | The `UNNotificationServiceExtension` shell, plus `NotifyResolver` — the pure failure ladder every branch of which is a banner someone reads |
| `NotifyCrypto.swift` | CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs` |
| `NotifyEnvelope.swift` | Envelope + payload parsing, base64url, `did:key` → SEC1, base58 |
| `NotifyKeychain.swift` | The shared-Keychain reads, and the pin document's shape |
| `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` | The bounded failure log the app surfaces in Settings |

### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)

Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.

`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens
`crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` (sealed by Rust's `hpke` crate) with
CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix carries no vector for this suite, so nothing else proves the two
agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The
fixture is referenced **in place** by the template — there is no copy here to drift.

## Dependencies

System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
process that runs on a locked screen.

## Key Decisions

- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.
- **Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain, not an app-group container.** The keychain group is
  already entitled and needs no Apple Developer portal work; an app group would be a second new
  entitlement on both bundles. The cost is that a push arriving before the first unlock after a
  reboot leaves no breadcrumb — the one failure that repairs itself, and the least worth
  recording.
- **The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id** in `scripts/ios/project.yml`. An app
  extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile, and signing secret; rendering
  one for admin-companion would cost a second set of those for an extension that cannot decrypt
  anything until MM-421 gives the console a shared keychain group and registered keys.

## Invariants

- The Keychain service name, account names, and both JSON document shapes in
  `NotifyKeychain.swift` / `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` are **copies** of constants in
  `apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/{keychain,notifications}.rs`. Two separate bundles can
  only agree by both spelling the same strings; a rename on one side is silent on the other.
- `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME` is pinned to `NotificationService` in the template. It is half of
  `NSExtensionPrincipalClass`, so a drift leaves iOS unable to instantiate the extension — a
  failure indistinguishable from a push that never arrived. `just ios-check` greps the pbxproj
  for it.
- The failure `reason` vocabulary (`NotifyFailureReason`) is shared with the app's
  `NotificationFailure.reason` and the frontend's `NotificationFailureReason`. Both readers

# Shared iOS Swift sources

Last verified: 2026-07-27

## Purpose

Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
notifications on arrival.

It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
inputs are shared too. MM-421 gives the operator console an extension from these same sources.

## Contracts

### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)

**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.

**Guarantees:**
- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.

**Expects:**
- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs` (MM-419).
- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `NotificationService.swift` | The `UNNotificationServiceExtension` shell, plus `NotifyResolver` — the pure failure ladder every branch of which is a banner someone reads |
| `NotifyCrypto.swift` | CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs` |
| `NotifyEnvelope.swift` | Envelope + payload parsing, base64url, `did:key` → SEC1, base58 |
| `NotifyKeychain.swift` | The shared-Keychain reads, and the pin document's shape |
| `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` | The bounded failure log the app surfaces in Settings |

### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)

Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.

`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens
`crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` (sealed by Rust's `hpke` crate) with
CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix carries no vector for this suite, so nothing else proves the two
agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The
fixture is referenced **in place** by the template — there is no copy here to drift.

## Dependencies

System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
process that runs on a locked screen.

## Key Decisions

- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.
- **Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain, not an app-group container.** The keychain group is
  already entitled and needs no Apple Developer portal work; an app group would be a second new
  entitlement on both bundles. The cost is that a push arriving before the first unlock after a
  reboot leaves no breadcrumb — the one failure that repairs itself, and the least worth
  recording.
- **The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id** in `scripts/ios/project.yml`. An app
  extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile, and signing secret; rendering
  one for admin-companion would cost a second set of those for an extension that cannot decrypt
  anything until MM-421 gives the console a shared keychain group and registered keys.

## Invariants

- The Keychain service name, account names, and both JSON document shapes in
  `NotifyKeychain.swift` / `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` are **copies** of constants in
  `apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/{keychain,notifications}.rs`. Two separate bundles can
  only agree by both spelling the same strings; a rename on one side is silent on the other.
- `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME` is pinned to `NotificationService` in the template. It is half of
  `NSExtensionPrincipalClass`, so a drift leaves iOS unable to instantiate the extension — a
  failure indistinguishable from a push that never arrived. `just ios-check` greps the pbxproj
  for it.
- The failure `reason` vocabulary (`NotifyFailureReason`) is shared with the app's
  `NotificationFailure.reason` and the frontend's `NotificationFailureReason`. Both readers
  tolerate an unrecognized value on purpose: the extension versions independently, and the entry
  a strict reader would drop is the one the user is asking about. A new case still needs wording
  in `apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/notification-health.ts`.
- CI gates: `just ios-template-check` (Linux — target present, gated, embedded, entitlements
  order and least privilege, sources exist) and `just ios-check` (macOS — the same facts in the
  generated pbxproj). Neither compiles Swift; `ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so the
  extension's own tests are a local/manual `xcodebuild test -scheme <app>_NSETests`.

old = "`NotificationsError` (SESSION_LOCKED, RATE_LIMITED, IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND, KEY_GENERATION_FAILED, KEYCHAIN_ERROR, SERVER_ERROR, NETWORK_ERROR) serialized as `{ code: \"SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE\" }` with camelCase fields"
new = ("A fourth command, `clear_notification_failures()`, and the `notification-failures` slot run the "
       "**other way**: the Notification Service Extension (`ios/NotificationService/`) appends to that slot "
       "and this module only reads it. iOS cannot let an extension suppress an alert push, so a payload that "
       "fails to verify still produces a banner — the honest \"couldn't verify\" notice, which on its own is a "
       "mystery. The breadcrumbs are what let Settings distinguish a key desync (open the app; it re-pins) from "
       "a relay sending junk (nothing at risk; consider another relay), which are the same banner and opposite "
       "responses. Read **fail-open** and with `reason` typed as a plain `String`: the extension is a separate "
       "bundle that versions independently, so an unrecognized reason must reach the screen generically rather "
       "than be dropped — the entry a stricter reader would discard is the one the user is asking about. "
       "`NotificationsError` (SESSION_LOCKED, RATE_LIMITED, IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND, KEY_GENERATION_FAILED, "
       "KEYCHAIN_ERROR, SERVER_ERROR, NETWORK_ERROR) serialized as `{ code: \"SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE\" }` with "
       "camelCase fields")
assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)

# 2. keychain accounts invariant
old2 = """`notification-sender-keys` (the versioned per-host pin document), and `notification-apns-token` (lowercase hex)."""
new2 = """`notification-sender-keys` (the versioned per-host pin document), `notification-apns-token` (lowercase hex), and `notification-failures` (the Notification Service Extension's bounded breadcrumb log — **the one slot the extension writes and the app only reads**, hence the same locked-screen protection class: a failure is recorded in the moment it happens, which is on a locked screen)."""
assert s.count(old2) == 1
s = s.replace(old2, new2)

# 3. key files: notifications.rs entry
old3 = "the Keychain half is tested against the in-memory double, including the protection class each slot lands under"
new3 = ("the Keychain half is tested against the in-memory double, including the protection class each slot "
        "lands under and the exact bytes the Swift extension writes into `notification-failures`")
assert s.count(old3) == 1
s = s.replace(old3, new3)

p.write_text(s)
print("wallet AGENTS.md patched")

1	# Shared iOS Swift sources
2	
3	Last verified: 2026-07-27
4	
5	## Purpose
6	
7	Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
8	thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
9	notifications on arrival.
10	
11	It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
12	`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
13	inputs are shared too. The operator console will grow an extension from these same sources when it
14	adopts notifications.
15	
16	## Contracts
17	
18	### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)
19	
20	**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
21	instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.
22	
23	**Guarantees:**
24	- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
25	  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
26	  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
27	  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
28	- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
29	  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
30	- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
31	  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.
32	
33	**Expects:**
34	- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
35	  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
36	  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
37	  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
38	- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
39	  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs`.
40	- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.
41	
42	| File | What it holds |

50	### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)
51	
52	Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
53	testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.
54	
55	`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens

58	agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The

61	## Dependencies
62	
63	System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
64	Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
65	process that runs on a locked screen.

67	## Key Decisions
68	
69	- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
70	  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.

1	// pattern: Mixed (Functional Core pin-store arithmetic; Imperative Shell commands + Keychain)
2	//
3	// The device half of the end-to-end-encrypted notification relay: the keys a Custos instance
4	// seals push payloads to, the registration that tells it where to send them, and the pinned
5	// sender-key set the Notification Service Extension verifies against.
6	//
7	//   register_for_notifications(did)         — POST /v1/notifications/register
8	//   refresh_notification_sender_keys(did)   — GET  /v1/notifications/sender-keys (the re-pin)
9	//   get_notification_diagnostics()          — what this device holds, for Settings
10	//   clear_notification_failures()           — acknowledge the extension's breadcrumbs
11	//
12	// Nothing here decrypts anything. The Notification Service Extension that does is a separate
13	// bundle (`ios/NotificationService/`, Swift + CryptoKit); this module's whole job is to leave
14	// the right material in the right Keychain slots under the right protection class, and to keep
15	// the pinned set fresh.
16	//
17	// # The one slot this module reads but does not write
18	//
19	// `notification-failures` runs the other way: the extension appends to it, the app reads it.
20	// It exists because iOS will not let a Notification Service Extension suppress an alert push,
21	// so a payload that fails to verify still produces a banner — the honest "couldn't verify"
22	// notice, which on its own is a mystery. The breadcrumbs are what let Settings say whether the
23	// cause is a key desync (the instance rotated and this device has not re-pinned) or a relay
24	// sending junk, which are the same banner and completely different problems.
25	//
26	// # Why the material is device-global rather than per-DID
27	//
28	// A push arrives at the extension as `{v, kid, enc, ct}` and nothing else — no DID, no handle,
29	// no account hint, because naming one would hand the relay and Apple the metadata the whole
30	// design exists to withhold. So the recipient key cannot be per-identity: the extension would
31	// have no way to choose among several. One device, one notification keypair, one `device_uuid`;
32	// every identity on the device registers the same public key with its own host.
33	//
34	// # Why the pinned set is per-host anyway
35	//
36	// `kid` is an autoincrement column on *one* Custos instance. Two instances will both publish a
37	// `kid` of 1 for entirely unrelated keys, and this wallet routinely holds identities on more
38	// than one. So the pin store is a map from hosting server to that server's published set, and
39	// the extension tries every candidate key registered under the incoming `kid`. That costs
40	// nothing and cannot go wrong: HPKE Auth mode either authenticates against a given sender key
41	// or it does not, so a wrong candidate fails closed and the next is tried. A single flat set
42	// keyed by `kid` alone would instead have two instances silently overwriting each other.
43	//
44	// # Re-pinning is wholesale replacement
45	//
46	// A successful fetch replaces that host's entry entirely rather than merging into it. That one
47	// choice is what implements all three rotation semantics from the design: a new key appears, a
48	// retired key stays as long as the server keeps publishing it, and a *revoked* key vanishes from
49	// this device the first time it contacts its Custos. Merging would keep a compromised key
50	// pinned forever, which is precisely the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close.
51	//
52	// A failed fetch changes nothing. An instance that answers 501 has not revoked anything — it has
53	// switched the feature off, or was never configured — and a 503 means it could not read its own
54	// keys. Treating either as "revoke everything" would let one bad deploy strip the pins off every
55	// device that happened to check in during it.

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && git add -A && git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit -F - <<'MSG'
Wallet: Notification Service Extension — decrypt-and-render + unverified notice

The receiving half of the encrypted notification relay. The device could already be
sealed to; it could not open what arrived, so every notification rendered as the
relay's placeholder.

Three things are worth reviewing carefully.

**The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id in a template shared by both
apps.** An app extension is a separate bundle: it needs its own App ID, its own
distribution profile, and its own signing secret before a signed build that embeds it
can be archived. Rendering `{{app.name}}_NSE` for admin-companion too would cost a
second set of those artifacts for an extension that cannot decrypt anything — the
console declares no keychain-access-groups and registers no notification keys, so its
extension would read an empty shared group and render the unverified notice for every
push. The gate uses handlebars-rust's built-in `eq` (registered in
`Registry::setup_builtins`, not a cargo-mobile2 helper, so it survives a tauri-cli
bump) against the same literal `just bundle-identity-check` already pins.

This does make the wallet's TestFlight lane a release blocker until that App ID and
profile exist; docs/ios-cicd.md now says so in the section that already anticipated it.
`just ios-pr-check` runs no xcodebuild and is unaffected.

**Failure is a rendering decision, not an error path.** iOS cannot let an extension
suppress an alert push, so "drop what we cannot verify" was never available — the only
thing under control is what the user reads. The rule is absolute: content that opened
under HPKE Auth mode renders as content, everything else renders as the explicit
unverified notice. That holds on the timeout path too, which is otherwise the one route
by which unverifiable text reaches the screen looking like the server's.

**Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain rather than an app-group container.** The
keychain group is already entitled and needs no portal work; an app group would be a
second new entitlement on both bundles. The cost is precise and small: a push arriving
before the first unlock after a reboot leaves no breadcrumb — but neither can the
extension read its key then, and that state repairs itself on unlock. The two failures
worth surfacing (key desync, a relay sending junk) happen on a device unlocked since
boot, where both stores work.

Settings reads them back and states the difference, because the lock-screen notice
cannot. The wording levels before it chooses: the worst severity in a seven-day window
wins, and the sentence comes from the reason most common *at that level* — so one
benign post-restart failure never becomes the sentence shown for a week that also holds
four key desyncs, and a week of only post-restart failures never manufactures an alarm.

`reason` is a plain string on both readers, deliberately. The extension is a separate
bundle that versions independently, and the entry a strict enum would drop is exactly
the one the user is asking about.

The Swift lives at the repo root, one implementation for both app lanes, the same shape
as scripts/ios/. Its logic tests compile the extension's sources rather than importing
them — an app extension has no testable module, since there is no TEST_HOST it can be
loaded into — and the fixture cross-check opens crates/crypto's golden HPKE vectors
with CryptoKit, which is what those vectors were generated for.

Not verified without a device: that a real sealed push from a live Custos renders, and
that the extension is instantiated at all. `ios-pr-check` runs no xcodebuild, so the
CryptoKit half is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme <app>_NSETests`; the template and
generated-project wiring are gated by `ios-template-check` and `ios-check`, and the
failure ladder, the levelling, and the Rust-side breadcrumb reader are covered by tests
that need neither.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && gh pr create --base main --head claude/mm-420-nse-decrypt-render-8c4f7c --title "Wallet: Notification Service Extension — decrypt-and-render + unverified notice (MM-420)" --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
Closes [MM-420](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-420/notify-69-wallet-notification-service-extension-decrypt-and-render). Phase 6 of the [notification relay](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311/e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-custos-apns); design in `docs/design-plans/2026-07-17-notification-relay-implementation.md`.

The receiving half. The device could already be sealed to — it could not open what arrived, so every notification rendered as the relay's placeholder.

## ⚠️ Release blocker before the next wallet TestFlight build

The extension is embedded into the app bundle, so from this change onward the wallet's TestFlight lane archives **two** bundles and needs a provisioning profile for each. Before `just ios-ipa` / `ios-testflight.yml` can sign again:

1. Register App ID `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService` (no capabilities to enable — `keychain-access-groups` rides the profile's `<TeamID>.*` wildcard, and there is no App Store Connect record: an extension ships inside its host app).
2. Mint a Distribution profile bound to it, signed by the **same** cert the wallet already uses.
3. Add its base64 as a GitHub secret alongside `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION`.

`just ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild` and is unaffected, so **this PR's gate is green today**. `docs/ios-cicd.md` now carries the full list in the section that already anticipated it.

## Three things worth reviewing carefully

**The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id, in a template shared by both apps.** An app extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile and secret. Rendering `{{app.name}}_NSE` for admin-companion too would cost a second set of those artifacts for an extension that cannot decrypt anything — the console declares no `keychain-access-groups` and registers no notification keys, so its extension would read an empty shared group and render the unverified notice for every push. Its own notification adoption is where the gate widens, in the same change that gives it a shared group.

The gate uses handlebars-rust's built-in `eq` (registered in `Registry::setup_builtins`, **not** a cargo-mobile2 helper, so it survives a tauri-cli bump) against the same literal `just bundle-identity-check` already pins — the two reinforce each other rather than compete.

**Failure is a rendering decision, not an error path.** iOS cannot let an extension suppress an alert push, so "drop what we cannot verify" was never on the menu; the only thing under control is what the user *reads*. The rule is absolute: content that opened under HPKE Auth mode renders as content, everything else renders as the explicit unverified notice. That holds on `serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire` too, otherwise the one route by which unverifiable text reaches the screen looking like the server's.

**Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain rather than an app-group container** (the issue text said app-group). The keychain group is already entitled and needs no portal work; an app group would be a second new entitlement on both bundles, stacked on the App ID above. The cost is precise: a push arriving before the first unlock after a reboot leaves no breadcrumb — but neither can the extension read its key then, and that state repairs itself on unlock. The two failures worth surfacing (key desync, a relay sending junk) happen on a device unlocked since boot, where both stores work.

## What landed

- **Template** (`scripts/ios/project.yml`): `{{app.name}}_NSE` (`app-extension`, Swift-only), its embed dependency, a `{{app.name}}_NSETests` logic-test bundle, and a dedicated test scheme that builds *only* the extension — attaching the tests to the app's scheme would have made the fixture cross-check cost a full Rust staticlib build every run.
- **Extension** (`ios/NotificationService/`, one implementation for both app lanes, same shape as `scripts/ios/`): CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode with suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs`; every candidate under the incoming `kid` tried across every pinned host (the push names no host, and Auth mode makes a wrong guess free); the sealed `ezpds` block stripped from the delivered notification.
- **Diagnostics**: `notification-failures` is the one Keychain slot the extension writes and the app only reads. Settings states the difference the lock-screen notice cannot — the wording **levels before it chooses**, so one benign post-restart failure never becomes the sentence shown for a week that also holds four key desyncs, and a week of only post-restart failures never manufactures an alarm.
- **Gates**: `ios-template-check` (target present, gated, embedded, entitlements order + least privilege, sources exist) and `ios-check` (the same facts in the generated pbxproj). Every one of those fails *silently* otherwise: the app installs and runs, and every notification says "couldn't verify" forever.

`reason` is a plain string on both readers, deliberately — the extension versions independently, and the entry a strict enum would drop is exactly the one the user is asking about.

## Verification

| | |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p identity-wallet` | 725 passed |
| `cargo clippy -p identity-wallet --all-targets -D warnings` | exit 0 |
| `pnpm check` / `pnpm test` (wallet) | 462 files 0 errors · 259 tests |
| `ios-template-check` · `ios-check` (syntax) · `ios-paths-check` · `bundle-identity-check` · `ticket-ref-check` · `docs-check` · `changelog-check` | pass |
| Template renders to valid YAML in both branches | wallet → 3 targets + embed + test scheme; admin → unchanged |
| Settings surface driven in the browser harness (new `notifications-unverified` scenario) | levelling, `role="alert"`, sr-only prefix, clear action, light + dark, no console errors |

**Not verified without a device:** that a real sealed push from a live Custos renders, and that iOS instantiates the extension at all. `ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so the CryptoKit↔Rust fixture cross-check is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme Obsign_NSETests` — the on-device demo in the issue's acceptance criteria remains outstanding for the same reason. The failure ladder, the levelling, and the Rust-side breadcrumb reader are covered by tests that need neither a device nor crypto.

* **Interop check:** on-device XCTest opens the `crates/crypto` golden fixtures with CryptoKit — the cross-implementation verification the fixtures were built for.

* On-device demo: sealed push from a real Custos renders decrypted content; junk/replayed-junk payload renders the unverified notice; fixture cross-check passes.

---
name: reference_ios_template_handlebars_context
description: What the shared XcodeGen template (scripts/ios/project.yml) can branch on — the cargo-mobile2 context keys and which handlebars helpers exist
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`scripts/ios/project.yml` is rendered per-app by cargo-mobile2's `bicycle`, whose handlebars
context is a **fixed** map built in `src/apple/project.rs` (`ios-frameworks`, `ios-valid-archs`,
`asset-catalogs`, `ios-additional-targets`, `ios-*-scripts`, `app.*`, `apple.*` …). There is no
free-form per-app key to hang a flag on.

**Per-app branching therefore goes through `{{#if (eq app.identifier "…")}}`.** `eq` (and
`ne`/`gt`/`and`/`or`/`not`/`len`) are **handlebars-rust built-ins**, registered unconditionally
in `Registry::setup_builtins` — *not* cargo-mobile2 helpers, so they survive a tauri-cli bump.
cargo-mobile2's own helpers are only `join`, `quote-and-join{,-colon-prefix}`, `html-escape`,
`snake-case`, `ident-{no-last,last}-part`, `escape-kotlin-keyword`, `dot-to-slash`,
`prefix-path`, `unprefix-path`. There is no `contains`, so list membership can't gate anything.

Path depth from `gen/apple/`: `../../..` = `apps/<app>/`, `../../../../..` = repo root, `../..` =
`apps/<app>/src-tauri/` (what a `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` value resolves against).

**Validate a template edit locally** — a broken template breaks `cargo tauri ios init` for
everyone and only surfaces on the macOS lane. Render both branches with a throwaway
mini-handlebars in python (resolve **inner** `#if`s before the outer gate, or a non-greedy regex
closes the gate at the wrong `{{/if}}`), then `ruby -ryaml -e 'YAML.load_file(...)'` — pyyaml is
not installed but macOS ruby has YAML.

Sources: `github.com/tauri-apps/cargo-mobile2` `src/apple/project.rs` + `src/templating/init.rs`;
`github.com/sunng87/handlebars-rust` `src/registry.rs`. Both fetched via the GitHub contents API
(raw.githubusercontent 404s for these).

Related: [[project_ios_framework_linking]], [[project_nse_appid_release_blocker]]

MM-420 is done and in review: **[PR #483](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/483)**.

## ⚠️ One action is on you before the next wallet release

The extension is embedded in the app bundle, so the TestFlight lane now archives **two** bundles and needs a profile for each. `just ios-ipa` will fail at signing until you:

1. Register App ID `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService` (no capabilities, no App Store Connect record)
2. Mint a Distribution profile bound to it, same cert as the wallet
3. Add its base64 as a GitHub secret alongside `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION`

`ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so PR gates stay green — this only bites at release. Full checklist is in [docs/ios-cicd.md](docs/ios-cicd.md).

## What shipped

- **Template** — `{{app.name}}_NSE` + embed + a test bundle and a scheme that builds *only* the extension, all gated to the wallet's bundle id
- **Extension** ([ios/NotificationService/](ios/NotificationService/)) — CryptoKit HPKE auth-mode open, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto`; every candidate under the incoming `kid` tried across every pinned host
- **Diagnostics** — the extension's breadcrumbs read back into a Settings section that names the cause
- **Gates** — `ios-template-check` (source) and `ios-check` (generated pbxproj)

## Two deviations from the issue text, both flagged in the PR

**Breadcrumbs → shared Keychain, not an app group** (your call earlier). It costs one thing precisely: a push arriving before first unlock after a reboot leaves no breadcrumb — but the extension can't read its key then either, and that state self-heals.

**Wallet-only NSE** (your call). Widening later costs a second identical set of Apple artifacts.

## Verification

725 Rust tests · clippy exit 0 · 462 files 0 type errors · 259 frontend tests · every Linux gate passing. I rendered the template for both apps and YAML-validated the output (wallet → 3 targets + embed + scheme; admin → unchanged), and drove the Settings surface in the browser harness through a new `notifications-unverified` scenario — levelling, `role="alert"`, the clear action, light and dark, no console errors.

**Not verified:** the on-device demo in the acceptance criteria. `ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so the CryptoKit↔Rust fixture cross-check is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme Obsign_NSETests`, and nothing here proves a real sealed push renders or that iOS instantiates the extension at all. The failure ladder, the levelling, and the Rust-side reader are covered by tests that need neither a device nor crypto — but the AC isn't closed until you run it on hardware.

One thing I got wrong mid-build and corrected: I'd documented seeding failures via `window.__harness.state()`, which returns a deep clone, so nothing happened. The scenario preset is the real mechanism, and the AGENTS.md note now says so.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

input.new_string:
# Typecheck the Notification Service Extension's Swift against the real iOS SDK — the
# extension's sources alone, then the test bundle exactly as the XcodeGen template composes
# it (extension sources compiled INTO the test target, since an app extension has no module
# to import).
#
# This exists because no other lane compiles Swift at all: `_pr-check` cross-compiles the
# Rust staticlib and stops, and the archive that would surface a Swift error only runs on
# push to main, holding signing secrets. Without this, a compile error in ~800 lines of
# security-critical Swift reaches TestFlight before anything objects — and the
# file-existence loop in ios-template-check would have to stand in for a compiler.
#
# `-typecheck`, not a build: it needs no simulator, no signing, and no generated Xcode
# project, so it runs on a bare checkout in seconds. macOS-only (xcrun); the caller is the
# macOS pr-check.
_nse-typecheck:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    sdk="$(xcrun --sdk iphonesimulator --show-sdk-path)"
    platform="$(xcrun --sdk iphonesimulator --show-sdk-platform-path)"
    # The deployment target is pinned to the same 17.0 both apps declare: CryptoKit's HPKE
    # auth-mode initializer does not exist before it, so a lower target here would let a
    # regression that raises the real minimum pass unnoticed.
    common=(-typecheck -sdk "$sdk" -target arm64-apple-ios17.0-simulator)
    xcrun swiftc "${common[@]}" ios/NotificationService/*.swift
    echo "✓ NSE sources typecheck"
    # XCTest's Swift overlay lives beside the framework, not inside it; without the -I the
    # C macros are found instead and every assertion reads as an unknown identifier.
    xcrun swiftc "${common[@]}" \
      -F "$platform/Developer/Library/Frameworks" \
      -I "$platform/Developer/usr/lib" \
      ios/NotificationService/*.swift ios/NotificationServiceTests/*.swift
    echo "✓ NSE test bundle typechecks"

1	// pattern: Mixed (Functional Core pin-store arithmetic; Imperative Shell commands + Keychain)
2	//
3	// The device half of the end-to-end-encrypted notification relay: the keys a Custos instance
4	// seals push payloads to, the registration that tells it where to send them, and the pinned
5	// sender-key set the Notification Service Extension verifies against.
6	//
7	//   register_for_notifications(did)         — POST /v1/notifications/register
8	//   refresh_notification_sender_keys(did)   — GET  /v1/notifications/sender-keys (the re-pin)
9	//   get_notification_diagnostics()          — what this device holds, for Settings
10	//   clear_notification_failures()           — acknowledge the extension's breadcrumbs
11	//
12	// Nothing here decrypts anything. The Notification Service Extension that does is a separate
13	// bundle (`ios/NotificationService/`, Swift + CryptoKit); this module's whole job is to leave
14	// the right material in the right Keychain slots under the right protection class, and to keep
15	// the pinned set fresh.
16	//
17	// # The one slot this module reads but does not write
18	//
19	// `notification-failures` runs the other way: the extension appends to it, the app reads it.
20	// It exists because iOS will not let a Notification Service Extension suppress an alert push,
21	// so a payload that fails to verify still produces a banner — the honest "couldn't verify"
22	// notice, which on its own is a mystery. The breadcrumbs are what let Settings say whether the
23	// cause is a key desync (the instance rotated and this device has not re-pinned) or a relay
24	// sending junk, which are the same banner and completely different problems.
25	//
26	// # Why the material is device-global rather than per-DID
27	//
28	// A push arrives at the extension as `{v, kid, enc, ct}` and nothing else — no DID, no handle,
29	// no account hint, because naming one would hand the relay and Apple the metadata the whole
30	// design exists to withhold. So the recipient key cannot be per-identity: the extension would
31	// have no way to choose among several. One device, one notification keypair, one `device_uuid`;
32	// every identity on the device registers the same public key with its own host.
33	//
34	// # Why the pinned set is per-host anyway
35	//
36	// `kid` is an autoincrement column on *one* Custos instance. Two instances will both publish a
37	// `kid` of 1 for entirely unrelated keys, and this wallet routinely holds identities on more
38	// than one. So the pin store is a map from hosting server to that server's published set, and
39	// the extension tries every candidate key registered under the incoming `kid`. That costs
40	// nothing and cannot go wrong: HPKE Auth mode either authenticates against a given sender key
41	// or it does not, so a wrong candidate fails closed and the next is tried. A single flat set
42	// keyed by `kid` alone would instead have two instances silently overwriting each other.
43	//
44	// # Re-pinning is wholesale replacement
45	//
46	// A successful fetch replaces that host's entry entirely rather than merging into it. That one
47	// choice is what implements all three rotation semantics from the design: a new key appears, a
48	// retired key stays as long as the server keeps publishing it, and a *revoked* key vanishes from
49	// this device the first time it contacts its Custos. Merging would keep a compromised key
50	// pinned forever, which is precisely the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close.
51	//

1	# iOS CI/CD — TestFlight
2	
3	**Last verified:** 2026-06-30
4	
5	## Overview
6	
7	CI/CD runs on **GitHub Actions**, split into two lanes by platform. The Linux PDS lane
8	(`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs the `just ci-pds` test gate, and Railway deploys the
9	PDS natively from GitHub (see [`docs/deploy.md`](deploy.md)). The `identity-wallet`
10	Tauri iOS app can't build on the Linux runners — `cargo tauri ios build` needs macOS +
11	Xcode + the Apple toolchain (this is exactly why `just ci-pds` builds the workspace with
12	`--exclude identity-wallet`), so it gets its own macOS lane.
13	
14	That macOS lane is this workflow. GitHub-hosted macOS runners (Apple Silicon) are **free
15	for public repositories**, so the cloud iOS lane costs nothing. The workflow builds a
16	signed App Store IPA and uploads it to **TestFlight**; you install/update the app from the
17	TestFlight app on your device.
18	
19	```
20	  git push main ──►  Actions: ci.yml             →  Railway: PDS staging/production   (Linux)
21	                ├─►  Actions: ios-testflight      →  TestFlight: Obsign               (macOS)
22	                └─►  Actions: admin-testflight    →  TestFlight: Admin Companion      (macOS)
23	```
24	
25	There are **two** iOS apps, each with its own macOS lane and TestFlight app: the
26	`identity-wallet` (Obsign) wallet and the `admin-companion` operator console. The runbook
27	below covers the wallet end-to-end; the [Admin Companion lane](#admin-companion-lane-second-ios-app)
28	section documents the (small) delta for the second app.
29	
30	The two lanes never overlap: the PDS lane proves the shared Rust core is correct on Linux
31	and ships the server; the iOS lane only proves the iOS-specific surface (cross-compile →
32	sign → package → ship).
33
